Altered cheque — a genuine, validly signed cheque whose payee or amount is changed.
Counterfeit cheque — the instrument itself is fabricated.

body.key: Forged maker = the DRAWER's signature is fake. Forged endorsement = the cheque was genuinely drawn, but the PAYEE's signature is fake. This pair is tested almost every sitting.

body.p: Exploiting the float — the gap between deposit and collection — by writing cheques against uncollected funds across two or more accounts to create fictitious balances. Tells: matched deposits/withdrawals between the same accounts, escalating amounts, heavy activity in low-balance accounts, frequent balance enquiries, and average daily float greatly exceeding the average ledger balance.

ul: Counterfeit / cloned cards from skimmed track data.
Card-not-present (CNP) — online/phone use of stolen numbers (now dominant).
Lost/stolen use; never-received issue (NRI) — intercepted in the mail.
Account takeover — change the address, then report the card lost for a replacement.
Bust-out — build a good record, max every line, disappear.
Merchant factoring — a complicit merchant launders another's transactions through its own account.
Carding — testing stolen numbers with small transactions before a large one.
Business email compromise (BEC) — spoofed/hijacked email redirecting a payment; the control is out-of-band verification of any account-detail change.
P2P fraud — irrevocable transfers induced by deception; no chargeback.
Cryptocurrency — pseudonymous, not anonymous; irreversible and cross-border, hence a laundering/ransom vector; traceable at exchange on/off ramps.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: kiting creates value out of float — the fraud is the timing gap, not the instrument. If the pattern shows two banks and matched round-trip cheques, it is kiting whatever else it resembles.

body.p: Place every procurement scheme at the correct phase of the contracting process. The exam distinguishes schemes chiefly by when in the cycle they occur.

body.h: The procurement phases and their schemes

ul: Presolicitation (need defined, specs written): need-recognition fraud (manufacturing an unnecessary purchase) and bid tailoring / specification fraud (specs written so only one favoured vendor qualifies).
Solicitation (bids invited): bid manipulation, bid rigging, leaking of bid data.
Bid evaluation & award: corrupt evaluation, manipulated scoring, unjustified sole-source award.
Post-award / performance: product substitution, defective pricing, cost mischarging, change-order abuse, progress-payment fraud.

body.key: Bid tailoring happens BEFORE the tender (in the specifications). Bid rigging happens DURING solicitation/evaluation. Same conspiracy goal, different phase — and the phase is the tested discriminator.

body.h: Collusion among bidders — the four named forms

ul: Complementary (cover/courtesy) bidding — competitors submit deliberately high or unacceptable bids to fake competition. The most common form; the losing bidders are participants, not victims.
Bid rotation — conspirators take turns being low bidder on a schedule.
Bid suppression — competitors agree to withdraw or not bid.
Market division — competitors carve up territories or customers and do not compete.
Product substitution — deliver lower-grade/non-conforming goods, bill for the specified grade.
Defective pricing — submit cost/pricing data that is not current, accurate, or complete, inflating a negotiated price.
Cost mischarging — charge costs to the wrong contract (often a cost-plus) or claim unallowable costs.
Change-order abuse — win low, then recover margin through inflated change orders (tell: abnormally low bid + abnormally many changes).
Progress-payment fraud — bill for completion stages not reached.
Grant fraud — funds diverted from the stated purpose; false progress reports.
Benefit/entitlement fraud — payments for ineligible or ghost recipients.
Conflict of interest — an official with an undisclosed interest in a bidder (complete on non-disclosure; no payment required).
Bribery of officials; bid-data leakage; revolving-door abuse (steering a contract to a future employer).

body.eye: Examiner's eye: complementary bidding is the answer whenever competitors submit bids they never intended to win, to manufacture the appearance of competition. Consistent losing margins plus a rotating winner is the statistical fingerprint — genuine competitors' estimates scatter; conspirators' do not.

body.p: Financial statement fraud (FSF) is the deliberate misrepresentation of an organisation's financial condition through intentional misstatement or omission, to deceive users who rely on the statements. It is the least frequent but most costly branch of occupational fraud. The line from aggressive accounting into fraud is crossed at material misstatement + intent to deceive.

body.h: The five scheme families — classify by mechanism

ul: Fictitious revenue — sales to fake, phantom, or non-existent customers; sham related-party sales.
Timing differences — real revenue or expense recorded in the wrong period (premature recognition, channel stuffing, bill-and-hold).
Concealed liabilities & expenses — omitting payables, warranty or litigation reserves; improperly capitalising operating costs.
Improper disclosures — omitting related parties, contingencies, subsequent events, or going-concern doubt (the numbers on the face may be correct; the notes hide the truth).
Improper asset valuation — inflating inventory, receivables, or fixed assets; failing to write down impaired assets.

body.key: 'December sales booked in November' = timing difference (real sale, wrong period). 'Sales to a shell customer that doesn't exist' = fictitious revenue. 'Failing to record warranty reserves' = concealed liabilities. The distinction is the whole game.

body.p: Improperly capitalising a routine operating expense (booking a repair as a fixed asset) overstates assets AND overstates net income in the current period, because the expense is deferred off the income statement. Watch for this exact two-part effect.

ul: Vertical (common-size) analysis — each line as a % of a base (sales for P&L, total assets for balance sheet). Best for an abnormal COGS-to-sales or margin shift.
Horizontal analysis — % change line-by-line across periods.
Ratio analysis — receivable and inventory turnover, gross margin, current ratio.
Cash-flow cross-check — revenue rising while operating cash flow lags is the master FSF red flag; genuine sales convert to cash, fictitious ones pile up as receivables.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: when revenue rises but operating cash flow lags, follow the receivables. Improper-disclosure fraud is the sneakiest — no number on the face is wrong, so read the related-party and subsequent-events notes against the transaction data.

body.p: Corruption is one of the three branches of occupational fraud. The exam tests whether you can place a scenario into the correct one of its four named forms — and the distinctions turn on timing, direction, and disclosure, not on the size of the payment.

ul: Bribery — giving or receiving a thing of value to influence a business decision. A kickback is a bribery variant where a vendor returns part of an overbilling to the employee who steered the deal.
Illegal gratuity — a thing of value given as a reward for a decision already made, with no prior agreement to influence it.
Economic extortion — the demand side: an employee (or official) demands a payment under threat, to decide in the payer's favour.
Conflict of interest — an undisclosed economic or personal interest in a transaction the employee influences, creating divided loyalty.

body.key: Bribery vs illegal gratuity turns entirely on timing/intent: bribery influences a future decision (quid pro quo agreed before); an illegal gratuity rewards a past decision with no prior agreement. Economic extortion is bribery's mirror — the recipient demands under threat rather than being offered.

body.h: Conflict of interest — the disclosure line

body.p: A conflict of interest becomes a fraud concern when the interest is undisclosed and the divided loyalty harms the employer. Crucially, no payment and no loss are required — the undisclosed interest is itself the violation. This is the single most common corruption trap on the exam.

ul: Complementary (cover) bids — deliberately high bids to fake competition.
Bid suppression — agreeing not to bid.
Bid rotation — taking turns being the low bidder.
Market division — splitting territories or customers.

body.p: Corruption is detected far more by tips and relationship analysis than by the books — the underlying transaction often looks normal. Map employee-vendor connections, unexplained lifestyle changes, exclusive-dealing patterns, and vendors that consistently win against stronger competitors.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: for bribery vs gratuity, find the moment of agreement. Agreed before the decision = bribery; given after with no prior deal = illegal gratuity. For extortion, ask who demanded and under what threat. For conflict of interest, ask only whether the interest was disclosed.

ul: Placement — dirty cash first enters the financial system (deposits, structuring/smurfing, cash-intensive fronts, buying monetary instruments).
Layering — complex transfers obscure the source (shell companies, wire chains, cross-border movement, conversion between asset types).
Integration — 'clean' funds re-enter the economy as legitimate-looking assets (real estate, businesses, luxury goods).

body.key: Order: Placement → Layering → Integration. Placement is the riskiest stage for the launderer, because that is where physical cash meets a reporting system.

body.p: Structuring — breaking a large cash sum into multiple sub-threshold deposits to evade currency-transaction reporting — is a placement-stage technique. Critically, structuring is an offence in itself even if the underlying cash is from a legal source, because the intent is to defeat the reporting requirement. The tell is many small, just-under-limit, often round-number deposits across days, branches, or people.

ul: FATF — issues the 40 Recommendations; the global AML/CFT standard-setter.
Egmont Group — links national Financial Intelligence Units (FIUs).
Wolfsberg principles (private-bank AML); Basel prudential guidance (distinct from AML).
Core obligations: KYC/CDD, enhanced due diligence for high-risk customers, currency-transaction reports (CTRs) and suspicious-activity reports (SARs).
Cash-intensive front businesses — mixing illicit cash with genuine receipts (integration via a legitimate-looking business).
Trade-based laundering — over- or under-invoicing trade to move value across borders under cover of legitimate commerce.
Shell and nominee structures — obscuring beneficial ownership during layering.
Casinos, cryptocurrency mixers, and monetary instruments — used to break the audit trail.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: structuring is about intent to evade a threshold, not the amount — the amount alone never proves it. And placement is where the cash enters; layering is the movement to obscure; integration is the return as apparent wealth. Match the described act to the stage.

body.p: Broader than 'a share'. Under the Howey test an investment contract exists where there is (1) an investment of money, (2) in a common enterprise, (3) with an expectation of profits, (4) derived predominantly from the efforts of others.

body.key: The fourth element is usually decisive: if the investor's own labour drives the return, it is not a security. The orange grove sold with a management contract was a security; the bare grove was not.

ul: Ponzi — earlier investors paid from later investors' principal; no real underlying investment. Collapses when redemptions exceed new money.
Pyramid — returns depend on recruiting. Distinguish from lawful MLM: the test is whether money comes from retail sales to genuine end users or from recruitment and inventory loading.
Pump and dump — accumulate a thinly traded stock, hype it, sell into retail demand, price collapses. Thin liquidity is essential.
Insider trading — trading on material AND non-public information in breach of a duty. Both elements required.
Churning — a broker over-trades a controlled account to generate commissions.
Front running — trading ahead of a large known client order.
Boiler room — high-pressure telephone sales of dubious securities.
Unsuitable recommendations — product mismatched to the client's risk profile or objectives.
Consistently smooth returns regardless of market conditions — real markets are not smooth.
Above-market returns with claimed low risk; secrecy or 'too complex to explain' strategy.
Difficulty withdrawing; pressure to reinvest.
Unregistered products, unlicensed sellers, self-custody of assets, no independent auditor.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: Ponzi = passive investors paid from later principal. Pyramid = investors paid for recruiting. The exam wants the mechanism, not the outcome — both are unsustainable.

body.p: Classify insurance fraud by who commits it: the policyholder/claimant, the agent/broker, the insurer itself, or an internal employee. The exam's answer options are usually built along this axis.

ul: Premium diversion — the agent collects premium and never remits it. The most common agent fraud; discovered only when a claim reveals no policy exists.
Churning — inducing replacement of policies within the same insurer to generate fresh commission.
Twisting — misrepresenting facts to induce a switch to another insurer.
Sliding — charging for coverage the client never requested or agreed to.
Fictitious/phantom policies — policies written on non-existent people to earn commission.

body.key: Churning = replacement within the SAME insurer. Twisting = induced switch to ANOTHER insurer. Sliding = coverage the client never agreed to. All three generate commission; the exam distinguishes them by mechanism.

ul: Vehicle — staged accidents ('swoop and squat'), owner give-ups (arranging theft/destruction of one's own vehicle), inflated repairs, phantom passengers.
Property — arson for profit (over-insurance, financial distress, valuables removed beforehand), inflated contents inventories.
Life — false death claims, concealed terminal illness on application, forged beneficiary changes.
Liability — staged slip-and-fall, exaggerated soft-tissue injury (hard to disprove).

Workers' compensation — premium fraud by the employer (understated payroll, misclassified workers), claimant fraud (injury off the job or malingering), and organised rings (lawyer + complicit doctor + 'capper' recruiting claimants).
Claim filed shortly after inception or a limit increase.
Claimant unusually familiar with claims terminology; over-eager to settle.
No police or fire report where one would be expected.
The same doctor or lawyer recurring across unrelated claims.
Documents that are too neat, sequential, or from a single source.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: 'the claim came shortly after a coverage increase' and 'the same medical provider appears on unrelated claims' are the two facts planted most often. Either points to a premeditated or organised scheme rather than opportunism.

body.p: For the exam this is largely a vocabulary and mechanism chapter. You do not need to be a technologist; you need to attach the right name to the described behaviour, and know what each attack actually compromises.

ul: Virus — attaches to a host file and requires user action to execute and spread.
Worm — self-replicating and self-propagating; needs no host file and no user action.
Trojan horse — masquerades as legitimate software; does not self-replicate.
Ransomware — encrypts data and demands payment for the key.
Spyware / keylogger — covertly records activity or keystrokes.
Rootkit — conceals an intruder's presence at a deep system level.
Logic bomb — dormant code triggered by a condition (a date, or the author's payroll record vanishing).
Botnet — compromised machines under one controller; the engine behind DDoS and spam.

body.key: Virus needs a host file AND user action. A worm needs neither. If it spread across the network overnight with nobody opening anything, it is a worm.

ul: Social engineering — still the most effective intrusion vector; people, not technology, are the weak point.
Phishing / spear phishing / whaling — mass, targeted, and executive-targeted.
SQL injection, cross-site scripting, buffer overflow — application-layer exploits.
Man-in-the-middle — interception and possible alteration of traffic in transit.
DoS / DDoS — exhausting capacity to deny service. Note: this attacks availability; no data is exfiltrated.
Credential stuffing — reusing breached passwords elsewhere; zero-day — exploiting an unpatched vulnerability.
Salami technique — slicing tiny amounts (rounding fractions) from many accounts.

body.p: The hardest cyber threat because access is legitimate. Watch for privilege creep (access accumulating across role changes), shared or generic administrator accounts (which destroy attribution), after-hours access without business reason, and continuing access by employees under notice of termination.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: DDoS compromises availability, not confidentiality. Any option describing 'stealing data by flooding a server with traffic' is wrong on the mechanism. And the CIA triad — Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability — is the frame for classifying what an attack actually harms.

body.p: This chapter is a taxonomy. The exam tests whether you can place a described scam in the correct named box, and whether you know the tactics that recur across all of them.

ul: Advance-fee scheme — payment demanded up front for a loan, prize, inheritance or windfall that never arrives. The umbrella for many others.
Reload / recovery-room scheme — returning to an already-defrauded victim, often posing as a recovery service, for a second bite.
Telemarketing fraud — high-pressure phone sales; victim lists ('sucker lists') are bought and sold.
Romance / relational fraud — a cultivated relationship, then a manufactured crisis requiring money. Among the highest-loss consumer frauds.
Work-at-home schemes — fees for kits or 'certification'; reshipping and money-mule variants make the victim an unwitting launderer.
Home-improvement / repair fraud, travel and vacation scams, charity fraud (spiking after disasters), credit-repair fraud.

body.key: Reloading is the term to remember: a fraudster contacting a victim who already knows their loss details is evidence of connection to the original fraud, not of legitimacy.

ul: Artificial urgency and a closing deadline.
Demand for an irrevocable payment method — wire, gift card, cryptocurrency, cash courier.
An appeal to secrecy — 'don't tell your bank or family, they'll try to stop you' — which exists solely to prevent intervention.
Reciprocity: a small gift or 'prize' creating obligation; manufactured authority via spoofed caller ID and fake credentials.

body.p: The data does not support the folk belief that the elderly are universally the most victimised. Older victims tend to suffer higher losses per incident (more assets, deliberately targeted), while younger, more online-active consumers report fraud more frequently. Frequency and severity are different measures.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: irrevocable payment plus enforced secrecy is the signature tactic across nearly every consumer scam. And treat any option asserting 'the elderly are the most frequently victimised' with suspicion — that conflates frequency with severity.

body.p: Bankruptcy fraud is fraud committed using the insolvency process — either to hide assets from creditors, or to loot a business behind the shield of the proceeding.

ul: Debtor — the person or entity that owes; creditor — secured or unsecured, with priority determining payment order.
Trustee — administers the estate, collects and liquidates assets, and investigates the debtor's affairs. The examiner's natural ally.
Examiner — appointed where fraud or mismanagement is suspected; investigates but does not administer the estate.
Debtor in possession — in a reorganisation, the debtor retains control with fiduciary duties to creditors.

body.key: Do not conflate trustee and examiner. The trustee administers and liquidates; the examiner only investigates.

ul: Concealment of assets — by far the most common: assets omitted from the schedules or transferred to relatives/shells before filing.
Bust-out — the most heavily tested: build credit, order large inventory on credit, liquidate it fast (often below cost, for cash), divert the proceeds, then file. Planned insolvency from the outset.
Petition mills — a 'service' that files bankruptcy on a distressed person's behalf and strips fees.
Multiple filings across jurisdictions or identities to delay creditors.
Fraudulent transfers / preferences — moving assets out or paying favoured creditors before filing.
False statements in the schedules — the charge most bankruptcy fraud is actually prosecuted under.
A sharp, unexplained surge in credit purchases shortly before filing.
Inventory sold below cost, for cash, or to related parties.
Recent property transfers to family members or newly formed entities.
Books and records 'lost' or destroyed; a change of business name, location, or management before filing.
Principals' lifestyle unaffected by the claimed insolvency.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: concealment of assets is the most common bankruptcy fraud; bust-out is the most tested. Concealment hides what exists; a bust-out manufactures the insolvency. The detectable moment in a bust-out is the credit surge, not the eventual failure.

body.h: The one distinction that governs the chapter

body.key: Tax avoidance = lawfully arranging affairs to minimise tax. Tax evasion = unlawfully concealing or misrepresenting to escape tax. The difference is legality and intent, never the size of the saving.

body.p: Proving evasion generally requires: (1) an additional tax due and owing, (2) an affirmative act of evasion — not mere omission — and (3) wilfulness, a voluntary and intentional violation of a known legal duty. Negligence, honest mistake, or good-faith misreading of a complex provision fails the wilfulness element.

ul: Understating income — omitted cash receipts, unreported side businesses, skimming before the books.
Overstating deductions — fictitious expenses, personal costs claimed as business, inflated valuations.
Improper allocation — shifting income to a lower-taxed entity, person, or jurisdiction without substance.
Offshore concealment — undisclosed foreign accounts, nominee and shell structures.
False books / two sets of records; destruction of records.
Transfer pricing abuse; payroll tax fraud (withholding but not remitting; misclassifying employees as contractors).
Stolen-identity refund fraud — a return filed in the victim's name to capture the refund; discovered when the genuine return is rejected as a duplicate.
Preparer fraud — inflated deductions (often without the client's knowledge) or diverted refunds.
Impersonation scams — callers posing as the revenue authority demanding irrevocable payment.

body.p: Direct evidence of unreported income is rare, so examiners use indirect methods: the net worth method (change in assets less liabilities, plus living expenses, less known reported income = imputed unreported income), the expenditures method, and the bank deposits method.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: if the facts stress an aggressive but disclosed structure, the answer is avoidance. If they stress concealment, false documents, or a second set of books, the answer is evasion. Look for the affirmative act.

body.p: Competitive intelligence is the lawful collection and analysis of publicly available information. Espionage is obtaining information through illegal or unethical means. The line is the method, not the value of what is learned — aggregating public filings, patents, job ads and trade-show material into a valuable conclusion remains lawful.

body.key: A trade secret requires: (1) independent economic value from not being generally known, (2) not readily ascertainable by proper means, and (3) the owner took reasonable measures to keep it secret. The third element is where most claims fail — however valuable the information, an unprotected 'secret' is not a trade secret at law.

ul: Insiders — the largest single source, especially departing or disgruntled employees with legitimate access.
Social engineering — pretexting staff into disclosure.
Physical — dumpster diving, stolen devices, unattended documents, shoulder surfing.
Electronic — intrusion, malware, unsecured cloud storage, USB exfiltration.
Aggregation of open sources — individually harmless public facts that together reveal a secret.

body.p: The favourite targets are not executives but those with access and no security training: salespeople, engineers at conferences, administrative staff — and above all, employees who are leaving.

ul: NDAs at hire, re-acknowledged at exit; classification and marking of confidential material (this is the 'reasonable measures' evidence).
Need-to-know access control; logging and alerting on bulk downloads.
Exit interviews addressing retained materials and device return.
Monitoring the 60–90 days preceding a departure, where exfiltration typically shows as a ramp-up.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: for espionage-versus-intelligence questions, ignore how valuable the information was and look only at how it was obtained. Deception, trespass, bribery or interception = espionage; public sources, however cleverly aggregated = lawful intelligence.

body.p: Under accrual accounting, revenue is recognised when it is earned and expenses when incurred — not when cash moves. Almost all financial-statement fraud lives in that timing gap. The accounting equation — Assets = Liabilities + Owners' equity — must always balance, which is why every fraudulent entry forces an offset somewhere.

body.key: Cash basis records when cash moves; accrual records when earned/incurred. The gap between the two is where premature revenue and deferred expense schemes hide.

body.h: The statements and what each reveals

ul: Balance sheet — position at a point in time; assets, liabilities, equity.
Income statement — performance over a period; revenue less expenses.

Statement of cash flows — actual cash movement, split into operating, investing and financing. The hardest statement to manipulate, which is why the cash-flow cross-check is the examiner's best FSF tool.
Statement of changes in equity — movements in owners' interests.
Vertical (common-size) — each line as a percent of a base (sales for P&L, total assets for balance sheet).
Horizontal — percentage change line-by-line across periods.
Ratio analysis — receivable and inventory turnover, gross margin, current ratio, days-sales-outstanding.

body.h: Why the equation matters to the examiner

body.p: Because every entry must balance, a fraudster who inflates revenue must also inflate an asset (usually receivables) or suppress a liability. That forced offset is the trail: find the implausible asset or the missing liability.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: the statement of cash flows is the least manipulable, because cash either arrived or it did not. When earnings and operating cash flow diverge persistently, believe the cash flow.

body.p: Disbursement schemes are on-book: the organisation's own funds leave through its accounting system on fraudulent documentation. These are the most common occupational frauds.

ul: Billing schemes — shell-company invoices, personal purchases, inflated or duplicate invoices. The most common and costly disbursement fraud.
Payroll schemes — ghost employees, falsified hours or commissions, inflated pay rates.
Expense reimbursement — mischaracterised, overstated, fictitious, or duplicate claims.
Cheque and payment tampering — forged maker, forged endorsement, altered payee, authorised-maker abuse. Unique because the fraudster prepares or alters the instrument itself.
Register disbursements — false refunds and false voids: a recorded transaction created to justify removing cash.

body.key: Shell vs pass-through: a pure shell bills for goods or services never delivered. A pass-through (turnaround) actually buys real goods, then resells them to the employer at an inflated markup. So 'a pass-through delivers nothing' is false.
Register disbursement is NOT skimming. A false refund is a recorded fraudulent transaction used to pull cash out; skimming records nothing at all.

ul: Ghost employees — distribute paycheques in person and reconcile to active HR records; no real person claims a ghost's pay.
Billing schemes — duplicate-invoice tests, round-dollar invoices, vendor addresses matching employee addresses, invoices clustered just below approval thresholds.
Expense fraud — mischaracterisation (a genuine personal purchase reported as business) is the most common variant.
Cheque tampering — positive pay, bank reconciliation by someone without cheque-signing authority.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: the fastest billing-scheme screens are duplicate invoices, round-dollar amounts, employee-matching vendor addresses, and invoices sitting just under an approval limit. Invoices clustered at 9,800 against a 10,000 threshold is not a coincidence.

body.h: What a fraud examination is — and is not

body.p: A fraud examination is a methodology for resolving a specific allegation from inception to disposition: gathering evidence, taking statements, writing reports, and testifying. It is not an audit. Audits are recurring and general; examinations are specific, allegation-driven, and non-recurring.

body.key: Predication is the totality of circumstances that would lead a reasonable, professionally trained and prudent person to believe a fraud has occurred, is occurring, or will occur. No examination begins without it — and neither does any admission-seeking interview or covert operation. Mere suspicion is not predication; an inquiry without predication is a 'fishing expedition'.

ul: Analyse the available data.
Create a hypothesis — assume a worst-case scenario consistent with the data.
Test the hypothesis against evidence.
Refine or amend as new facts emerge.

body.key: Two golden rules of sequencing: conduct the examination general → specific, and interview least-culpable → most-culpable, so you reach the prime suspect last, armed with corroborated evidence.

ul: A fraud response plan is prepared in advance, defining who does what when an allegation arises — it is not drafted during a crisis.
Initial response: secure and preserve evidence, limit who knows, avoid alerting the suspect, and assess whether the allegation has predication.
Structure the investigation to preserve confidentiality — restrict the team, use need-to-know, and run the work at the direction of counsel to protect privilege.
Consider from the outset: legal exposure, insurance/fidelity bond notification requirements, regulatory reporting duties, and recovery options.

body.p: Forensic accounting is the broader use of accounting skills in matters that may end in litigation (including valuation, damages, and bankruptcy work). Fraud examination is the narrower discipline of resolving fraud allegations. Every fraud examination may involve forensic accounting; not every forensic accounting engagement is a fraud examination.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: write down your predication before you act. If you cannot articulate why a reasonable professional would suspect fraud, you are not ready to begin — and opposing counsel will make that point later. When a question offers 'begin the admission-seeking interview' as an early step, it is almost always wrong.

body.h: Public power versus private power — the core distinction

body.key: Constitutional criminal protections (search and seizure, self-incrimination, Miranda warnings) primarily restrain government action. A private employer is not required to give Miranda warnings before interviewing an employee. Private employers still face limits from employment law, contract, policy, defamation, false imprisonment, and privacy law.

ul: Garrity — a public employee cannot be compelled to give self-incriminating statements under threat of dismissal; statements so compelled cannot be used criminally.
Weingarten — a unionised employee may request a representative at an investigatory interview reasonably likely to result in discipline.
Employment-at-will and duty of loyalty — employees generally owe a duty of cooperation, but compelled cooperation has limits.
Agency/state action — a private examiner acting at the direction of law enforcement may become a state actor, importing constitutional constraints that would not otherwise apply.

body.h: Risks that attach to private investigations

ul: False imprisonment — detaining an employee against their will, blocking exit, or implying they may not leave.
Defamation — publishing an unproven allegation to third parties without privilege.
Invasion of privacy — intrusion into areas where the employee has a reasonable expectation of privacy (personal lockers, bags, personal devices) absent policy and notice.
Wrongful/constructive dismissal and malicious prosecution where referral was made without reasonable grounds.
Publish and acknowledge policies that reduce the expectation of privacy in company systems and property.
Keep interviews voluntary in fact and in appearance — the door unlocked, the employee told they may leave.
Confine communication of allegations to those with a legitimate need to know.
Run the investigation at the direction of counsel to preserve privilege and to calibrate legal risk.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: the exam repeatedly tests whether you know that Miranda does not apply to private employers — but equally that this does not make anything permissible. The correct answer usually preserves voluntariness and confidentiality rather than asserting unlimited employer power.

body.h: The four common-law elements of fraud

body.key: (1) A material false statement, (2) knowledge of its falsity when made, (3) reliance on it by the victim, and (4) resulting damages. All four are required. Memorise them — they recur throughout the section.

body.p: 'Material' and 'reliance' do real work. A false statement nobody relied on, or one too trivial to have influenced the decision, will fail the legal test even where the conduct feels dishonest.

body.h: Principal types of fraud in law

ul: Larceny — wrongful taking of property from another's possession with intent to permanently deprive.
Embezzlement — fraudulent conversion of property by someone to whom it was lawfully entrusted. The distinction from larceny is that possession was originally lawful.
False pretences / obtaining property by deception — obtaining title by a false representation of past or existing fact.
Conversion — a civil wrong: exercising dominion over another's property inconsistent with their rights.
Breach of fiduciary duty — violating a duty of loyalty and care owed to a principal.
Conspiracy — an agreement between two or more to commit an unlawful act, usually requiring an overt act in furtherance.

body.key: Larceny vs embezzlement turns on how possession began: unlawful taking from the outset = larceny; lawful entrustment then conversion = embezzlement. False pretences transfers title, not merely possession.

body.h: Key statutes the exam tests by trigger phrase

ul: 'Pattern of racketeering activity' → RICO (criminal penalties plus civil treble damages).
'Whistleblower sues on the government's behalf and shares the recovery' → qui tam under the False Claims Act.
'CEO/CFO certification of financial statements; document-destruction penalties' → Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX).

'Bribing a foreign official to obtain or retain business; books-and-records and internal-control provisions' → FCPA. (The UK Bribery Act is broader — it covers private-to-private bribery and 'failure to prevent'.)
'Scheme to defraud using the mail or wires' → mail and wire fraud statutes.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: these statutes are tested as recognition, not litigation. Lock one trigger phrase to each. And when a scenario turns on whether possession was lawful at the outset, the answer is the larceny/embezzlement distinction.

ul: Testimonial — statements made under oath by a witness.
Real (physical) — tangible objects; documents are usually treated as documentary, a sub-class of real evidence.
Demonstrative — charts, models, and summaries prepared to explain other evidence. Demonstrative evidence illustrates; it is not itself proof of the underlying fact.

body.key: Direct evidence proves a fact without inference (an eyewitness who saw the act). Circumstantial evidence requires an inference (fingerprints, a pattern of transactions). Most fraud cases are built largely on circumstantial evidence — and that is fully valid and admissible. Circumstantial is not 'weaker': a document trail is often more reliable than a nervous eyewitness.

ul: Evidence must be relevant (tends to prove or disprove a fact in issue), material, and competent (reliable, properly obtained).
Hearsay — an out-of-court statement offered for the truth of its contents — is generally excluded, subject to exceptions (notably business records made in the regular course of business).
The best evidence rule generally requires the original document where the contents are in issue.
Even relevant evidence may be excluded where its prejudicial effect substantially outweighs its probative value.

body.p: An unbroken, documented record of everyone who handled an item, when, and for what purpose. A documented gap can render evidence inadmissible — the opposing party need only show the item could have been altered. Record receipt, transfer, storage, and return in an evidence log.

ul: Attorney-client privilege — protects confidential communications between lawyer and client for the purpose of legal advice.
Work-product doctrine — protects materials prepared in anticipation of litigation.
Running an investigation at the direction of counsel is the practical step that preserves both.
Impeachment — attacking a witness's credibility (prior inconsistent statements, bias, capacity, prior convictions where permitted).

body.eye: Examiner's eye: any option asserting that fraud 'requires direct evidence' or that circumstantial evidence is inadmissible is wrong. And when a question describes a gap in handling, the answer is chain of custody — the risk is inadmissibility, not merely embarrassment.

ul: Obtain originals where possible; if only copies are available, document why.
Maintain an evidence control log and chain-of-custody record for every item.
Handle documents minimally to preserve fingerprints, indented writing, and ink/paper characteristics.
Never write on, highlight, or annotate an original — it destroys evidentiary integrity.
Store in protective sleeves; avoid stapling, folding, or exposing to heat and light.
Handwriting comparison requires adequate known standards (exemplars). Prefer collected (naturally written, pre-dispute) standards over requested ones, which can be deliberately disguised.
Indented writing — impressions from a sheet written above, recoverable by electrostatic detection.
Dating a document — ink, paper, watermark, and typeface analysis can show a document could not have existed on its purported date.
The document examiner reports on authorship and alteration; they do not opine on the writer's intent.

ol: Preserve — image the media using a write-blocker; never work on the original.
Verify — compute and record hash values (MD5/SHA) before and after; matching hashes prove the image is bit-for-bit identical and unaltered.
Analyse the forensic copy — recover deleted files, slack space, metadata, logs, USB insertion artefacts.
Document tools, versions, and every step, maintaining chain of custody for digital media exactly as for physical.

body.key: The single most consequential mistake is booting or browsing the original device. Doing so changes last-access times, temp files, and logs — and can get your best evidence excluded. Image first, always.

body.p: Cloud data raises jurisdiction, multi-tenancy, and provider-cooperation issues; the data may reside in another country under different law. Mobile devices require specialist tools and carry volatile data — isolate the device from the network (airplane mode or a Faraday bag) to prevent remote wiping before imaging.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: 'analyse the image, never the original' and 'matching hash proves integrity' are near-certain questions. For mobile, the tested point is network isolation to prevent a remote wipe.

body.p: Fraud usually hides in the aggregate, not in any single transaction. Data analysis lets the examiner test entire populations rather than samples — which is why it detects schemes that transaction-by-transaction review never will.

ol: Define the objective — what scheme or hypothesis is being tested.
Obtain and verify the data — confirm completeness and integrity before analysing (control totals, record counts, date ranges).
Cleanse and normalise — resolve formats, duplicates, and inconsistencies.
Analyse — apply the tests appropriate to the hypothesis.
Validate and follow up — treat every hit as a lead requiring verification, never as a conclusion.

body.key: Verifying data completeness and integrity before analysis is the step candidates skip. An analysis run on incomplete or mis-parsed data produces confident, wrong answers.

ul: Duplicate testing — same invoice number, amount, date, or vendor.
Gap testing — missing sequential numbers in cheques or invoices.
Just-below-threshold analysis — transactions clustered under an approval limit.
Matching — vendor addresses or bank accounts against employee records.
Benford's Law — see below.
Outlier and trend analysis; textual analytics on emails and free-text fields; visual analytics and link analysis to expose relationships.

body.key: In naturally occurring numbers, leading digit 1 appears about 30.1% of the time, declining to about 4.6% for 9. It applies to natural numbers arising from underlying processes (invoice and payment amounts). It does not apply to assigned or sequential numbers (telephone, account, employee ID, cheque numbers), nor to figures constrained by a floor or ceiling. A deviation flags where to look — it never proves guilt.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: two guaranteed points here — Benford applies to natural amounts, not assigned numbers; and any analytic hit is a lead requiring verification, not a conclusion. Options that treat an anomaly as proof are wrong.

body.key: Public records are available to anyone, usually without the subject's consent (court filings, property records, corporate registries, liens, bankruptcies). Nonpublic records require consent, legal process, or a permissible purpose (bank records, tax returns, medical records, credit reports, telephone records). Accessing nonpublic records without authority creates civil and criminal exposure.

ul: Court records — prior litigation, judgments, divorces (often revealing assets), criminal history.
Property records — ownership, transfers, mortgages, liens; the chain of title that exposes daisy chains and hidden transfers.
Corporate/business filings — directors, registered office, shareholdings; the fastest route to employee-vendor connections.
UCC/security filings — secured lending and pledged collateral.
Regulatory and licensing bodies; tax and assessment rolls; vital records.
Nongovernment sources — trade associations, credit bureaus (permissible purpose required), media archives, social media.

body.p: Data protection and privacy laws restrict collection and use of personal data; financial-privacy laws restrict access to bank records; credit-reporting laws limit credit reports to permissible purposes. Pretexting to obtain financial records is unlawful in many jurisdictions — obtaining nonpublic data by deception is not a shortcut, it is an offence.

ul: Record the date, URL and method of every online capture; pages change and vanish.
Preserve with screenshots and, where possible, hashes — an unauthenticated printout is weak evidence.
Corroborate social media identity before relying on it; profiles are easily spoofed.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: the tested line is public versus nonpublic, and the trap is an option suggesting a pretext call to a bank. Obtaining nonpublic financial records by deception is unlawful — the correct answer uses consent, subpoena, or lawful process.

body.key: Direct method — follow specific transactions through the records ('follow the money'). Used when records are available and reliable. Indirect (circumstantial) methods — used when records are incomplete, destroyed, or income is unreported; they infer hidden funds from the subject's financial behaviour.

ul: Net worth method — (change in assets less liabilities) + living expenses − funds from known legitimate sources = imputed unreported income. The headline method.
Expenditures (sources and applications) method — compares total spending against known income; the excess implies undisclosed funds. Best where the subject spends rather than accumulates.
Bank deposits method — total deposits, less transfers between accounts and known legitimate sources, implies understated income. Best where the subject runs funds through accounts.

body.key: Choose by behaviour: the subject who accumulates assets → net worth method. The subject who spends everything → expenditures method. The subject who cycles cash through accounts → bank deposits method.

ul: Establish a firm starting net worth at a fixed date, or the whole computation is attackable.
Eliminate likely non-taxable or legitimate sources — gifts, inheritances, loans, prior cash hoards. The 'cash hoard' defence is the classic challenge.
Corroborate living expenses; do not merely estimate them.
Property and vehicle registries, corporate filings, court and divorce records, UCC/security filings.
Nominee holdings in the names of relatives, associates, and shell entities.
Lifestyle indicators, travel patterns, safe-deposit boxes, and offshore structures.
Asset recovery options: civil judgment and enforcement, freezing/restraint orders, constructive trusts, and criminal forfeiture.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: the net worth method is the most-tested tracing technique. Watch for questions that hinge on which indirect method fits the subject's behaviour, and for the 'unexplained wealth' fact pattern that signals net worth.

body.h: The five question types — in sequence

ol: Introductory — establish rapport, give a reason for the interview, obtain a commitment to cooperate. Never accuse here.
Informational — gather the facts; move open → closed → leading.
Closing — confirm facts, seek additional information, maintain goodwill.
Assessment — establish credibility and evaluate deception. Used only when needed.
Admission-seeking — only where there is reasonable certainty of guilt.

body.key: Sequence: Introductory → Informational → Closing → Assessment → Admission-seeking. The last two are conditional, not routine. Accusing during the introductory phase forfeits the informational phase you have not yet mined.

ul: Open — invites narrative ('Tell me what happened'). Yields the most information.
Closed — specific, often yes/no; used to pin down detail.
Leading — contains its own answer ('You were in the vault that night, weren't you?'); used to confirm what is already known.
Avoid compound and double-negative questions; they produce ambiguous answers that are useless in evidence.
Inhibitors — competing demands on time, ego threat, etiquette, trauma, forgetting, chronological confusion.
Facilitators — fulfilling expectations, recognition, altruistic appeals, sympathy, extrinsic rewards, catharsis.
The interviewer manages these deliberately: reduce inhibitors, supply facilitators.

body.p: Interview one subject at a time, privately, without an audience that would raise ego threat. Document contemporaneously. Do not reveal the extent of the evidence early. Keep the tone neutral and non-accusatory until the admission-seeking phase, if it is reached at all.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: the introductory phase is not small talk — it determines whether the subject cooperates at all. Any option that accuses early, interviews in a group, or opens with leading questions is wrong.

body.p: Only where there is reasonable certainty of guilt, supported by adequate predication, conducted privately by an interviewer of suitable standing. It is never the opening move and never a fishing exercise.

ol: Direct accusation — stated with confidence as a statement, not a question.
Observe the reaction; repeat the accusation.
Interrupt denials — stop them before they harden; a firmly stated denial is much harder to retract.
Establish a rationalisation — offer a morally acceptable theme to lower resistance.
Diffuse alibis; display evidence as needed.
Alternative question — two incriminating choices, one more face-saving ('Did you plan this, or did it just get out of hand?').
Obtain a benchmark admission, then escalate to a full confession.
Obtain a signed written statement.

body.key: The alternative question is the pivotal technique, and interrupting denials before they entrench is equally tested. Both appear almost every sitting.

ul: In the subject's own words, not the examiner's legal phrasing.
Include approximate dates, amounts, and the method; state intent; acknowledge voluntariness.
The subject should read and sign each page; corrections initialled by the subject.
Never promise leniency or non-prosecution — it exceeds the examiner's authority and can void the confession.

body.p: No single verbal or non-verbal cue proves deception. Clusters matter: answering a question with a question, over-qualifying, selective memory, character testimony ('I'd never do that'), and inconsistency with established facts. Treat cues as signals to probe, never as proof.

Truthful accounts tend to contain more unstructured production, contextual detail, unexpected complications, and spontaneous corrections; fabricated accounts are often chronologically tidy, sparse in sensory detail, and reluctant to admit memory failure.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: any option in which the examiner promises leniency, drafts the statement in legal language, or accuses without reasonable certainty of guilt is wrong. The alternative question always presents two incriminating choices — an option offering an innocent alternative is a distractor.

body.key: A covert operation requires adequate predication and a written memorandum prepared before it begins, setting out the basis, objectives, expected information, known suspects, and duration. Covert work is high-risk and is a last resort, not a starting point.

ul: Stationary (fixed-point), moving (tailing), and electronic surveillance.
Conduct only in places where the subject has no reasonable expectation of privacy. Surveillance into a home, or through a window, invites privacy claims.
Maintain a detailed surveillance log — times, locations, observations, and the identity of the observer — contemporaneously.

Electronic surveillance and recording are heavily regulated; consent requirements vary by jurisdiction (one-party versus all-party consent). Unlawful recording can be criminal and will taint the investigation.
A source provides information from their normal occupation without confidentiality expectations; an informant provides information on a confidential basis, often with motive or exposure of their own.
Assess motive — revenge, financial gain, or self-protection — and corroborate everything independently.
Protect identity carefully, but never promise absolute confidentiality that cannot be delivered if a court compels disclosure.
Document what was said, when, and by whom; do not direct an informant to commit unlawful acts or to obtain information you could not lawfully obtain yourself.

body.p: Establishing a false identity carries substantial legal and safety risk: entrapment allegations, personal danger, and civil liability. Undercover work should be used only where other methods have failed, with defined objectives, supervision, and an exit plan.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: the tested points are the written memorandum and predication before commencement, that surveillance must respect reasonable expectations of privacy, and that an examiner must never promise a source confidentiality the law may override.

ul: Accurate, clear, impartial, relevant, and timely.
Report facts and the evidence supporting them — not conclusions of law, and never an opinion on guilt.
Write for a reader who may be a judge, a jury, or opposing counsel: every sentence should survive being read aloud in court.

body.key: The four most-tested reporting errors: (1) stating legal conclusions or opining on guilt or innocence; (2) editorialising — inserting personal opinion, sarcasm, or characterisation of the subject; (3) omitting exculpatory evidence; (4) overstating findings beyond what the evidence supports.

body.p: Omitting exculpatory evidence is the most damaging: it hands opposing counsel a devastating cross-examination and destroys the examiner's credibility on everything else in the report.

ul: Background and how the matter arose; scope (and any limitations on it).
Procedures performed; findings supported by identified exhibits.
Summary; supporting schedules, exhibits and an index.
Avoid including opinions on guilt, recommendations for prosecution phrased as legal conclusions, or unnecessary personal details about individuals.

body.p: Charts, timelines and flow-of-funds diagrams are demonstrative aids: they must accurately represent the underlying evidence and be traceable to the exhibits they summarise. A chart that overstates or simplifies beyond the evidence is a liability, not an asset.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: if an option has the examiner writing 'the suspect is guilty of embezzlement' or leaving out evidence favourable to the subject, it is wrong. Report what was found; let the trier of fact decide what it means.

s_legalsystem.title: The Legal System, Criminal & Non-Criminal Actions

body.key: Lowest to highest: preponderance of the evidence ('more likely than not', civil) → clear and convincing evidence → beyond a reasonable doubt (criminal). This ladder is one of the most-tested items in the whole section.

ul: Criminal — brought by the state; purpose is punishment; standard is beyond a reasonable doubt; outcome is conviction and sentence.
Civil — brought by a private party; purpose is compensation or other remedy; standard is preponderance; outcome is judgment, damages, injunction, restitution.
Parallel proceedings — both may run at once. Manage self-incrimination exposure and discovery conflicts carefully.
The lower civil standard is why a defendant can be acquitted criminally yet still lose the civil case on the same facts.
Common law — judge-made precedent, adversarial procedure.
Civil law — codified statutes, inquisitorial procedure with a more active judge.
Administrative proceedings — regulatory bodies with their own procedures and sanctions (licences, penalties, debarment).

ol: Charging — by indictment or information; grand jury in some systems.
Arraignment and plea; pre-trial motions including suppression.
Trial — prosecution case, defence case, verdict.
Sentencing, then appeal on questions of law.
Corporate criminal liability — an organisation can be liable for acts of employees within the scope of employment intended to benefit it.

ul: Pleadings → discovery → trial → judgment; discovery (depositions, interrogatories, document production) is where most fraud cases are actually won.
Remedies: compensatory and punitive damages, restitution, constructive trust, injunction, rescission.
Alternative dispute resolution — arbitration (binding determination) and mediation (facilitated settlement, non-binding).
Internal organisational actions — discipline, dismissal, and recovery under fidelity bonds.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: 'more likely than not' → preponderance → civil. And remember that acquittal in a criminal case does not bar a civil action on the same facts, because the standards differ.

body.key: A lay witness testifies to facts personally observed. An expert witness, once qualified by the court, may offer opinions within their area of expertise. Qualification depends on knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education — and the opposing party may challenge it (voir dire).

A fraud examiner must never express an opinion on the legal guilt or innocence of any person. That determination belongs to the trier of fact, and offering it breaches the ACFE Code of Professional Ethics as well as damaging credibility.

ul: Review the report, working papers, and exhibits thoroughly; know the basis for every opinion.
Meet counsel in advance to understand the questions and anticipated cross-examination.
Ensure every opinion has a reasonable evidential basis — the Code requires it.
Bring only materials you are prepared to have opposing counsel examine; anything taken to the stand may be discoverable.
Listen to the whole question; pause; answer only what is asked. Do not volunteer.
Speak to the trier of fact in plain language; explain rather than impress.
Concede what is genuinely true — conceding a fair point preserves credibility; fighting an obvious one destroys it.
Stay within your expertise; if you do not know, say so.
Do not advocate. The examiner is a witness, not a member of the legal team.

body.p: Attacks on qualifications, on the completeness of the work (what you did not examine), on bias (who is paying you), on assumptions underlying the analysis, and rapid-fire leading questions designed to produce a yes/no answer that distorts the truth. The answer to the last is to insist, politely, on giving a complete answer.

body.eye: Examiner's eye: two guaranteed points — an expert may give opinions within their expertise, and no examiner may opine on legal guilt. When a question asks 'so the defendant is guilty?', the correct answer restates the findings and leaves the conclusion to the court.

s1q1.t: Under accrual accounting, when is revenue properly recognized?
o: When cash is received from the customer
When it is earned, regardless of when cash changes hands
At the end of the fiscal year
s1q1.e: Accrual accounting recognizes revenue when it is earned and expenses when incurred, independent of cash timing. Most financial-statement fraud abuses this earned-vs-cash gap to book revenue prematurely.

s1q2.t: A company records December sales in November to hit a quarterly target. Which financial-statement fraud family is this?
s1q2.e: Recording real transactions in the wrong period is a timing difference (premature recognition). Fictitious revenue involves fake/phantom customers; here the sales are real but mis-timed.

s1q3.t: Which occupational-fraud category has the LOWEST frequency but the HIGHEST median loss?
s1q3.e: Financial statement fraud is the rarest category but causes the largest median losses. Asset misappropriation is the inverse — most frequent, smallest median loss.

s1q4.t: An analyst expresses each income-statement line as a percentage of total sales to spot anomalies. This is:
s1q4.e: Vertical analysis states each line as a percent of a base (sales for the income statement, total assets for the balance sheet). Horizontal analysis compares percent change across periods.

s1q5.t: Aggressive-but-legal accounting becomes fraud when it crosses which line?
o: When it is material AND made with intent to deceive users
s1q5.e: The dividing line is material misstatement plus intent to deceive users who rely on the statements. Estimates and aggressive choices alone are not fraud without that intent and materiality.

s1q6.t: An employee rings 'no sale' and pockets a customer's cash. No entry is ever made. This is:
s1q6.e: Theft of cash before it enters the books is skimming (off-book). Because nothing was recorded, there's no direct audit trail — the defining feature versus larceny.

s1q7.t: The key distinction between skimming and cash larceny is:
o: Whether the cash was recorded before being stolen
Whether it occurred at a register
s1q7.e: Skimming = before recording (off-book); cash larceny = after recording (on-book). Larceny creates a discrepancy between records and cash on hand; skimming does not.

s1q8.t: An employee steals Customer A's payment, then applies Customer B's later payment to A's account to hide it, rolling the shortfall forward. This is:
s1q8.e: Lapping is the classic receivables-skimming concealment: crediting one customer with another's payment and continually rolling the gap forward.

s1q9.t: Which is a common red flag specifically suggesting lapping?
o: Customer complaints that payments were misapplied or late-posted
s1q9.e: Lapping produces misapplied/delayed customer payment postings, so customer complaints about their account status are a key tell. Independent reconciliation and confirmations help detect it.

s1q10.t: Which control most directly prevents cash-receipts skimming?
o: Segregation of duties between cash receipt, recording, and reconciliation
s1q10.e: Segregation of duties — the person who receives cash should not also record and reconcile it — is the core preventive control for receipts schemes.

s1q11.t: Fraudulent disbursement schemes are best described as:
o: On-book schemes where company funds are paid out via fraudulent documentation
A form of financial statement fraud
s1q11.e: Disbursements are on-book: the organization's funds leave through its own system using false documents (invoices, timesheets, expense claims, checks).

s1q12.t: A fake vendor that delivers no goods submits invoices that the colluding employee approves. This is a:
s1q12.e: A shell company billing scheme bills for goods/services never delivered. A pass-through differs because it actually buys goods then resells to the employer at an inflated price.

s1q13.t: Which disbursement scheme is unique because the fraudster physically prepares or alters the payment instrument itself?
s1q13.e: Check/payment tampering involves preparing or altering the instrument (forged maker/endorsement, altered payee), distinguishing it from schemes that only falsify supporting documents.

s1q14.t: A cashier records a false refund to justify removing cash from the register. This recorded transaction makes it:
s1q14.e: A register disbursement (false refund/void) is a recorded fraudulent transaction used to remove cash — distinct from skimming, where nothing is recorded.

s1q15.t: Ghost-employee schemes fall under which category?
s1q15.e: A ghost employee (a fake or terminated person kept on payroll) is a classic payroll fraudulent-disbursement scheme.

s1q16.t: Stacking empty boxes to make a warehouse look fully stocked during a count is:
s1q16.e: Physical padding conceals inventory theft by faking the quantity on hand during a physical count.

s1q17.t: The primary red flag for inventory theft is:
s1q17.e: Shrinkage — the unaccounted-for reduction in inventory — is the primary red flag. Fraudsters try to keep it within 'normal' ranges to avoid scrutiny.

s1q18.t: A buyer rewards a vendor with a contract AFTER the award, with no prior agreement to influence the decision. This is:
s1q18.e: An illegal gratuity rewards a decision already made, without a prior intent to influence. Bribery requires intent to influence a future decision.

s1q19.t: An employee demands a payment from a vendor in exchange for favorable treatment. This is:
s1q19.e: When the employee demands payment (the coercive, demand side), it is economic extortion. A kickback is typically initiated by the vendor returning part of an overbilling.

s1q20.t: A conflict of interest becomes a fraud concern primarily when:
o: The employee's interest is undisclosed and harms the employer
s1q20.e: The fraud trigger is an undisclosed economic/personal interest that creates divided loyalty harming the employer. Disclosure is the dividing line.

s1q21.t: A loan booked in a straw borrower's name for the real party's benefit is a:
s1q21.e: A nominee/sham loan uses a straw borrower to disguise the true beneficiary, often to evade lending limits or hide the real risk.

s1q22.t: Inflating a property's value to support a larger mortgage is best classified as:
s1q22.e: Appraisal fraud inflates the valuation to justify a larger loan — your ValuGuard domain. An 'air loan' is on a wholly nonexistent property/borrower.

s1q23.t: Which body sets global prudential standards for sound banking risk management referenced in the manual?
o: The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision
s1q23.e: The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision sets global prudential/risk-management standards for banks. FATF sets AML standards; Egmont links FIUs.

s1q24.t: The correct order of the money-laundering stages is:
s1q24.e: Placement → Layering → Integration. Dirty cash enters the system, is obscured through complex transfers, then re-enters as apparently legitimate assets.

s1q25.t: Breaking a large cash sum into multiple sub-threshold deposits to avoid reporting is:
s1q25.e: Structuring/smurfing is a placement-stage technique to evade currency-transaction reporting thresholds — exactly the self-transfer/sub-threshold signal your StaffLens flags.

s1q26.t: Which organization issues the 40 Recommendations that form the global AML/CFT standard?
s1q26.e: The Financial Action Task Force (FATF) issues the 40 Recommendations — the international AML/CFT benchmark adopted by national regimes (including India's PMLA framework).

s1q27.t: At which stage are 'clean' funds reintroduced into the economy as legitimate-looking assets?
s1q27.e: Integration is the final stage, where laundered funds appear as legitimate wealth (real estate, businesses, luxury assets).

s1q28.t: Exploiting the float between two banks by writing checks against insufficient funds is:
s1q28.e: Check kiting exploits the float (clearing delay) between accounts/banks to create artificial balances from non-existent funds.

s1q29.t: An attacker impersonates a CFO by email to redirect a vendor payment to a fraudulent account. This is:
s1q29.e: Business email compromise (BEC) uses impersonation of an executive/vendor to redirect payments — heavily emphasised in the 2026 cyberfraud blueprint.

s1q30.t: Which best distinguishes a Ponzi scheme from a pyramid scheme?
o: Ponzi pays earlier investors from new investors' funds; pyramids derive income chiefly from recruitment
s1q30.e: A Ponzi pays 'returns' from new investors' money (no real underlying returns). A pyramid generates income primarily from recruiting new participants rather than product sales.

s1q31.t: Tax evasion differs from tax avoidance because evasion:
o: Requires willful intent to illegally escape tax
s1q31.e: Tax evasion is illegal and requires willful intent to defeat tax. Tax avoidance uses lawful means to minimize tax. The intent/legality line is the tested distinction.

s1q32.t: A cashier removes cash that was already recorded as a sale, creating a drawer shortage. This is:
s1q32.e: Theft of already-recorded cash is cash larceny (on-book), evidenced here by the drawer shortage — the discrepancy skimming never produces.

s1q33.t: Complementary (cover) bids, bid suppression, and bid rotation are forms of:
s1q33.e: These are collusive bid-rigging techniques in procurement fraud, undermining genuine competition.

s1q34.t: Capitalizing a routine operating expense to boost current income is an example of:
s1q34.e: Improperly capitalizing an expense defers it off the income statement, understating expenses/liabilities and overstating income — a concealed-liabilities/asset-valuation manipulation.

s1q35.t: Which is the MOST frequent occupational-fraud category overall?
s1q35.e: Asset misappropriation is the most frequent occupational fraud (though it has the lowest median loss). Corruption is mid-range; FSF is rarest but costliest.

s3q1.t: The three legs of the Fraud Triangle are pressure, opportunity, and:
s3q1.e: Cressey's Fraud Triangle: pressure + opportunity + rationalization. Remove any leg and fraud becomes less likely. (Capability is the Fraud Diamond's added element.)

s3q2.t: Which model adds 'capability' to the Fraud Triangle?
s3q2.e: The Fraud Diamond adds capability — the individual's position, skills, and confidence to commit and conceal the fraud.

s3q3.t: Sutherland's definition of white-collar crime emphasizes crime committed by:
o: A person of respectability and high status in the course of their occupation
s3q3.e: Edwin Sutherland defined white-collar crime as crime committed by a person of respectability and high social status in the course of their occupation.

s3q4.t: According to ACFE research, the most common method by which occupational fraud is initially detected is:
s3q4.e: Tips are consistently the #1 detection method, which is why reporting hotlines are among the most effective anti-fraud controls.

s3q5.t: Primary responsibility for designing and maintaining internal controls rests with:
s3q5.e: Management owns the design and operation of internal controls and is primarily responsible for preventing and detecting fraud. Auditors provide assurance, not the controls.

s3q6.t: Which governance body most directly oversees financial reporting, internal control, and the external auditor?
s3q6.e: The audit committee (ideally independent directors) oversees financial reporting integrity, internal controls, and the external auditor relationship.

o: The ethical climate set by leadership's example and messaging
s3q7.e: Tone at the top is the ethical climate established by leadership. A weak tone is the strongest cultural fraud-risk factor.

s3q8.t: How many components are in the COSO Internal Control–Integrated Framework?
s3q8.e: COSO has five components: control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information & communication, and monitoring activities.

s3q9.t: Which is the foundational component of the COSO framework?
s3q9.e: The control environment (integrity, ethical values, tone at the top, governance) is the foundation on which the other components rest.

s3q10.t: Separating authorization, recording, and custody of assets is the control known as:
s3q10.e: Segregation of duties divides authorization, recording, and custody so no one person controls a whole transaction. Its absence is the most-cited control weakness.

s3q11.t: An unqualified ('clean') external audit opinion means:
o: No fraud exists in the company
Reasonable—not absolute—assurance the statements are free of material misstatement
s3q11.e: An audit provides reasonable, not absolute, assurance. A clean opinion is not a guarantee that no fraud exists — a classic exam distractor.

s3q12.t: In a fraud risk assessment, inherent risk is assessed:
s3q12.e: Assess inherent risk first (before controls), then factor in mitigating controls to determine residual risk. Likelihood × significance drives prioritization.

s3q13.t: A fraud risk assessment should be:
o: A periodic, ongoing process responsive to business changes
Performed only after a fraud occurs
s3q13.e: FRA is periodic and ongoing, updated as the business and risk environment change — not a single annual checkbox.

s3q14.t: Managing vendor and customer fraud risk through due diligence and audit rights addresses:
s3q14.e: Due diligence, ongoing monitoring, and contractual audit rights manage third-party fraud risk — your VendorRecon/DMA-scoring territory.

s3q15.t: Per ACFE research, which anti-fraud control is associated with faster detection and lower losses?
s3q15.e: Reporting hotlines are linked to faster detection and lower losses because tips are the leading detection method.

s3q16.t: Under the ACFE Code of Professional Ethics, a CFE shall:
o: Express an opinion on legal guilt when confident
Never express an opinion on the legal guilt or innocence of any person
Keep all findings secret from the client
s3q16.e: A core CFE Code duty: never express an opinion on the legal guilt or innocence of any person. Offer findings within expertise only.

s3q17.t: The CFE Code requires that any opinion rendered be supported by:
s3q17.e: A CFE must obtain evidence providing a reasonable basis for any opinion. Unsupported or speculative opinions violate the Code.

s3q18.t: Which statement about legality and ethics is correct?
o: An action can be legal yet still unethical
s3q18.e: Legal does not always mean ethical. Fraud examiners must distinguish morality, ethics, and legality and apply professional ethical standards beyond the legal minimum.

s1n1.t: Priya, an accounts-receivable clerk, steals a $4,000 check from Customer A. When Customer B pays $4,000 two weeks later, she posts B’s payment to A’s account, then covers B with Customer C. Which scheme and concealment is this?
o: Cash larceny concealed by a forced balance
A billing scheme concealed by a shell company
Register disbursement concealed by a false void
s1n1.e: The receivable was stolen before being fully accounted for and the shortfall is rolled customer-to-customer — the textbook signature of skimming concealed by lapping. A forced balance relates to register/cash counts, not receivables rolling.

s1n2.t: Which of the following is the BEST example of a fraudulent disbursement rather than skimming?
o: A waiter fails to ring up a cash sale and keeps the money
A clerk pockets cash from a recorded sale, creating a drawer shortage
An employee sets up a fake vendor and approves its invoices for payment
A cashier voids a legitimate sale and keeps the cash before recording it
s1n2.e: A fake-vendor (shell company) billing scheme is an on-book fraudulent disbursement — company funds leave through the AP system on false documentation. The cash-sale options are skimming (unrecorded) or larceny.

s1n3.t: TRUE or FALSE: Because skimming occurs before the transaction is recorded, it generally leaves a clear audit trail in the victim’s books.
s1n3.e: False. Skimming is off-book — the sale or receipt is never recorded, so it leaves no direct audit trail. That absence of a record is exactly what makes it hard to detect.

s1n4.t: A controller capitalizes routine repair costs as fixed assets to inflate current-year earnings. This MOST directly results in:
o: Overstated assets and overstated net income
No effect on the financial statements
s1n4.e: Capitalizing an expense moves it off the income statement onto the balance sheet — assets are overstated and net income is overstated because the expense was improperly deferred.

s1n5.t: Which financial-statement fraud scheme is committed by failing to record warranty or litigation reserves?
s1n5.e: Omitting required reserves (warranties, litigation, returns) understates obligations — a concealed liabilities and expenses scheme. The company looks more solvent and profitable than it is.

s1n6.t: Ravi ships goods to a distributor near period-end that the distributor has the unconditional right to return, and books the full sale immediately to hit targets. This is BEST described as:
s1n6.e: Pushing product into a channel near period-end to recognize revenue that may be returned is channel stuffing — an improper timing/premature-revenue scheme. Right-of-return undermines the ‘earned’ criterion.

s1n7.t: All of the following are red flags of financial statement fraud EXCEPT:
o: Revenue growing faster than cash flow from operations
A dominant CEO who overrides controls
Consistent dividends paid from stable, growing operating cash flow
s1n7.e: Stable, growing operating cash flow funding dividends is a sign of health, not fraud. The other three (revenue outpacing cash, receivables outpacing sales, control override) are classic FSF red flags.

s1n8.t: An employee buys a personal laptop and submits it on an expense report disguised as ‘client supplies.’ This is which type of expense-reimbursement scheme?
s1n8.e: A genuine purchase that is personal but reported as business is a mischaracterized expense. Overstated inflates a real business cost; fictitious invents one; duplicate claims the same cost twice.

s1n9.t: Which control would MOST effectively detect a ghost-employee scheme?
o: Requiring two signatures on the bank account
Periodically distributing paychecks in person and reconciling to HR records
s1n9.e: In-person paycheck distribution reconciled to HR/active-employee records exposes ghosts — no real person claims the check. Signature controls and encryption don’t reveal a fictitious payee.

s1n10.t: Vendor Sigma overbills ABC Ltd by $50,000 and returns $20,000 to the purchasing manager who approved it. The $20,000 is BEST classified as:
s1n10.e: A vendor returning part of an inflated payment to the employee who steered the business is a kickback — a form of bribery tied to overbilling/contract steering.

s1n11.t: The KEY element that distinguishes bribery from an illegal gratuity is:
o: The dollar value of the payment
Whether intent existed to influence a decision before it was made
Whether the recipient is a government official
Whether the payment was in cash
s1n11.e: Bribery requires intent to influence a decision (a quid pro quo before the act); an illegal gratuity rewards a decision already made with no prior agreement to influence. Value and form are irrelevant to the distinction.

s1n12.t: Three competing vendors agree in advance who will submit the lowest bid on each upcoming contract, taking turns. This is:
s1n12.e: Taking turns being the designated low bidder is bid rotation. Complementary (cover) bids are deliberately high to create an illusion of competition; suppression is agreeing not to bid.

s1n13.t: In the ICICI HFC context, a borrower obtains a loan in his gardener’s name but takes the proceeds and makes the payments himself. This is a:
s1n13.e: A loan booked in a straw borrower’s name for the true party’s benefit is a nominee/straw-borrower loan, often used to evade exposure limits or hide the real risk.

s1n14.t: An appraiser, paid by the loan officer, values a property at ₹1.2 crore when comparable sales support ₹70 lakh, enabling a larger mortgage. The PRIMARY scheme is:
s1n14.e: Inflating the valuation to justify a larger loan is appraisal fraud — directly your ValuGuard domain. An air loan involves a wholly nonexistent property or borrower.

s1n15.t: TRUE or FALSE: Under most AML regimes, structuring deposits to stay below a reporting threshold is itself a violation even if the underlying cash is from a legal source.
s1n15.e: True. Structuring (deliberately breaking deposits to evade reporting) is an offense in its own right regardless of the funds’ origin, because the intent is to defeat the reporting requirement.

s1n16.t: A customer deposits large cash sums, immediately wires them to several offshore shell companies, which then route funds back to buy local real estate. The offshore wiring stage corresponds to:
s1n16.e: Moving funds through shells and cross-border wires to obscure their origin is layering. The initial cash deposit is placement; buying the real estate at the end is integration.

s1n17.t: Which body issues the 40 Recommendations that serve as the global AML/CFT standard?
s1n17.e: FATF issues the 40 Recommendations. The Basel Committee handles prudential banking standards; the Egmont Group links national Financial Intelligence Units.

s1n18.t: Mr. Khan writes checks between his accounts at two different banks to exploit clearing delays and create the illusion of funds. This is:
s1n18.e: Exploiting the float between banks by passing checks against insufficient funds is check kiting.
