c17_j3.e: Exfiltration almost always shows a ramp-up in the weeks before departure — bulk transfers, unusual printing, after-hours access. This is precisely why exit procedures that begin on the last day detect nothing; the evidence sits in the preceding quarter's logs.

c17_d1.t: Investigator A obtains a rival's data by telephoning its help desk posing as an IT contractor. Investigator B obtains equivalent insight from the rival's published regulatory filings. These are, respectively:
o: Espionage (via pretexting) and lawful competitive intelligence
c17_d1.e: Obtaining information through a false identity is pretexting — a deceptive method, hence espionage. Reading published filings is lawful competitive intelligence. Identical information; the method determines legality.

c17_s1.scenario: A speciality chemicals firm discovers that its lead formulation chemist resigned on a Friday and began work at a direct competitor the following Monday. IT logs show that over the preceding eleven weeks he transferred unusually large volumes of files to a personal cloud account outside working hours and printed the master formulation binder twice. The firm required all technical staff to sign NDAs, marked the formulations 'Confidential — Restricted', and limited access to a need-to-know list on which he appeared.
c17_s1.t: Assess the firm's trade-secret position and the evidentiary picture:
o: Weak — no physical property was removed
Strong — all three trade-secret elements are satisfied, and the pre-departure activity ramp evidences misappropriation
Weak — the chemist had authorised access, defeating any claim
Strong only if the competitor actually used the formulations
c17_s1.e: All three elements are met: economic value from secrecy, not readily ascertainable, and reasonable measures (NDAs, confidentiality marking, need-to-know access). Authorised access does not license misappropriation, no physical removal is required for digital exfiltration, and actual use by the competitor is not an element of the claim. The eleven-week ramp is the evidentiary spine.

c17_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, which fact would MOST have weakened the firm's position had it been different?
o: If the competitor were in a different country
If the firm had never required NDAs, never marked the formulations confidential, and left access unrestricted
If the chemist had resigned with longer notice
If the transfers had occurred during working hours
c17_s2.e: Without NDAs, confidentiality marking, or access restriction, the third trade-secret element — reasonable measures — collapses, and there is no protectable trade secret however obvious the taking. Notice period, timing of transfers, and the competitor's location affect evidence or remedy, not the existence of the right.

c18_j1.t: Under accrual accounting, when is revenue properly recognised, and why does this matter to a fraud examiner?
o: When the invoice is issued, because that fixes the date
At the end of the fiscal year, for consistency
When it is earned regardless of cash timing — and almost all revenue fraud exploits the gap between earning and collection
When cash is received, because cash is objective
c18_j1.e: Accrual recognises revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, independent of cash. Nearly all revenue-recognition fraud lives in that gap — booking revenue before it is earned. Invoice issuance alone does not establish that revenue was earned, and year-end timing is irrelevant to recognition.

c18_j2.t: Which financial statement is generally the HARDEST for management to manipulate, and what follows for the examiner?
o: The statement of cash flows; so when earnings and operating cash flow persistently diverge, weight the cash flow
The statement of changes in equity; so trace dividends
The balance sheet; so verify assets first
The income statement; so recompute revenue
c18_j2.e: The statement of cash flows is hardest to manipulate — cash either arrived or it did not. That is precisely why a persistent divergence between reported earnings and operating cash flow is the strongest FSF signal, and why the examiner weights cash flow over accrual-based figures.

c18_j3.t: A fraudster inflates reported revenue. Because the accounting equation must balance, what necessarily follows, and how does the examiner exploit it?
o: An offsetting asset must be inflated (typically receivables) or a liability suppressed — so look for the implausible asset or missing liability
Nothing follows; revenue is independent of the balance sheet
Cash must increase by the same amount
c18_j3.e: Every entry balances, so inflated revenue forces an offsetting inflated asset (usually receivables) or a suppressed liability. That forced offset is the trail — which is why receivables ballooning faster than sales is such a reliable indicator. Cash need not increase (indeed, in fictitious revenue it does not).

c18_d1.t: Analyst A expresses every income-statement line as a percentage of sales for each of three years. Analyst B computes the percentage change in each line from year to year. These are, respectively:
c18_d1.e: Vertical (common-size) analysis states each line as a percent of a base within a period. Horizontal analysis measures change across periods. Vertical exposes an abnormal margin or COGS shift; horizontal exposes an abnormal growth rate.

c19_d1.t: Employee A sets up a company that invoices her employer for consulting never performed. Employee B sets up a company that genuinely buys components and resells them to the employer at a 40% markup, without disclosing her ownership. These are, respectively:
o: A pass-through scheme and a shell-company scheme
A shell-company scheme and a pass-through (turnaround) scheme
c19_d1.e: A shell bills for goods or services never delivered. A pass-through delivers real goods but at an inflated markup through an undisclosed intermediary. The common error is assuming a pass-through delivers nothing — it does deliver; the fraud is the markup and concealed ownership.

c19_d2.t: A cashier rings a sale, then processes a false refund and removes the cash. Another cashier takes cash from a sale and never rings it at all. These are, respectively:
o: A register disbursement scheme and skimming
c19_d2.e: A false refund is a recorded transaction created to justify removing cash = register disbursement (on-book). Taking cash with no entry at all = skimming (off-book). The discriminator is whether a fraudulent record was created — register disbursements leave one, skimming leaves none.

c19_j1.t: Which control is MOST effective at detecting a ghost-employee scheme?
o: Requiring two signatures on the payroll bank account
Periodically distributing paycheques in person and reconciling recipients to active HR records
c19_j1.e: In-person distribution reconciled to active HR records exposes ghosts directly — no real person appears to claim a fictitious employee's pay. Signature controls, encryption, and auditor rotation do nothing to reveal that a payee does not exist.

c19_j2.t: An examiner has time for one analytic across a year of accounts-payable data. Which combination is MOST likely to surface a billing scheme?
o: Duplicate-invoice testing, round-dollar detection, vendor-address matching against employee addresses, and clustering of invoices just below approval thresholds
c19_j2.e: Those four tests target the structural signatures of billing fraud: duplicates, artificial round amounts, vendors sharing an employee's address, and invoices deliberately sized just under an approval limit. Depreciation, bank balances, and dividends have no bearing on fraudulent vendor payments.

c19_j3.t: What makes cheque and payment tampering distinct from the other disbursement families?
o: It can only be committed by managers
The fraudster prepares or alters the payment instrument itself, rather than only falsifying supporting documentation
c19_j3.e: Tampering is unique because the fraudster physically prepares or alters the instrument — forging the maker's or payee's signature, or changing the payee or amount. The other families falsify supporting documents (invoices, timesheets, expense claims) to induce a legitimate-looking payment.

c19_s1.scenario: A construction firm's internal audit reviews payments to subcontractors. One vendor, registered eighteen months ago, has been paid 340,000 across 41 invoices. The vendor has no website, no telephone listing, and a registered address that matches the home address of a project manager's spouse. Every invoice was approved by that same project manager, each falls between 8,200 and 9,600 against a 10,000 approval threshold, and none is supported by a delivery note, site log entry, or inspection record. No site worker recalls the subcontractor attending.
c19_s1.t: The scheme and its two clearest structural signatures are:
o: Cheque tampering; forged maker and altered payee
Payroll fraud; ghost employees and inflated rates
Expense reimbursement fraud; mischaracterised and duplicate claims
A shell-company billing scheme; the vendor-address match to an employee's household and invoices deliberately clustered just below the approval threshold
c19_s1.e: A vendor with no operational footprint, an address matching an employee's household, invoices approved solely by that employee, no evidence of work performed, and amounts clustered just under the approval limit is a textbook shell-company billing scheme. The threshold clustering is deliberate structuring to avoid higher-level review. No instrument was altered, and no payroll or expense claim is involved.

c19_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, which control failure most directly enabled the scheme?
o: The same individual could both select the vendor and approve its invoices, with no independent verification that work was performed
The approval threshold was set too high in absolute terms
Invoices were submitted on paper rather than electronically
The firm used subcontractors at all
c19_s2.e: The scheme required one person to control both vendor selection and invoice approval, with no independent confirmation of delivery — a segregation-of-duties failure. Threshold level is secondary (the fraudster simply sized invoices to fit); using subcontractors and paper invoices are normal business practices, not control failures.

c19_d3.t: Employee A buys a personal laptop and submits it on an expense report as 'client supplies'. Employee B submits the same genuine taxi receipt twice in two months. These are, respectively:
o: A mischaracterised expense and a duplicate reimbursement
An overstated expense and a fictitious expense
c19_d3.e: A genuine purchase that is personal but reported as business = mischaracterised expense (the most common variant). Submitting the same real receipt twice = duplicate reimbursement. Overstated inflates a real business cost; fictitious invents one that never occurred.

p1_j1.t: An anonymous tip alleges a warehouse manager is diverting stock. Inventory shrinkage at his site has risen while other sites are stable. Which is the MOST appropriate first step?
o: Confront the manager directly to gauge his reaction
Document the predication, then plan an examination proceeding from the general (the stock process) to the specific (the manager)
Interview the manager's subordinates about his character
p1_j1.e: The tip plus corroborating shrinkage data gives predication, which must be documented before acting. The examination then proceeds general → specific, examining the process before the person. Confronting the suspect first (an admission-seeking step) destroys the informational phase and is premature; character interviews are not evidence; suspension pre-judges the matter.

p1_j2.t: Which statement BEST captures why interviews should proceed from least-culpable to most-culpable witnesses?
o: It reduces the total number of interviews required
It is required by law in most jurisdictions
It allows the examiner to reach the prime suspect last, holding corroborated evidence, and avoids alerting them prematurely
Junior employees are more likely to be truthful
p1_j2.e: Sequencing least-to-most culpable means the examiner accumulates corroborated facts before confronting the suspect, and avoids tipping them off to destroy evidence or align stories. It does not reduce interview volume, is a professional methodology rather than a legal requirement, and makes no assumption about junior staff honesty.

p1_j3.t: A CFO says 'I have a bad feeling about the new procurement clerk — nothing specific, but look into everything she's touched.' What is the MOST appropriate response?
o: Explain that a generalised suspicion without supporting circumstances lacks predication, and seek specific facts or analytics before opening an examination
Place the clerk under covert surveillance to develop facts
Interview the clerk immediately to see if she confesses
Begin a full examination; management has authorised it
p1_j3.e: A vague feeling is not predication — it is precisely the 'fishing expedition' the standard forbids, regardless of who authorises it. Management approval does not supply predication. Covert operations and admission-seeking interviews require more predication, not less, so both are worse.

p1_d1.t: Engagement A is a recurring annual review of controls and financial statements across the whole entity. Engagement B resolves a specific allegation that a named employee falsified expense claims. These are, respectively:
o: An audit and a fraud examination
A fraud examination and an audit
p1_d1.e: Audits are recurring and general in scope; a fraud examination is specific, allegation-driven and non-recurring, resolving a particular matter from inception to disposition. The discriminator is scope and trigger, not who performs the work.

p1_d2.t: An examiner reviews shipping data, forms the theory that a manager is diverting goods, then tests that theory against gate logs which contradict it, and revises the theory. Which steps of the fraud theory approach are illustrated, in order?
o: Analyse data → create hypothesis → test hypothesis → refine/amend
Create hypothesis → analyse data → test → refine
p1_d2.e: The fraud theory approach runs analyse available data → create a hypothesis (worst-case) → test it → refine or amend. The facts here follow exactly that order: data review, theory, contradiction on testing, revision. Hypothesising before analysing inverts the method.

p1_s1.scenario: A finance director tells an internal examiner that a payables clerk 'has been acting oddly' and should be investigated. On enquiry, the director cannot identify any specific transaction, discrepancy, or complaint; he explains the clerk recently bought a car and has become withdrawn. No analytics have been run. The director asks the examiner to review all of the clerk's emails and to interview her the same afternoon about possible theft.
p1_s1.t: The MOST appropriate course of action is to:
o: Proceed as directed — the finance director has authority over the function
Interview the clerk informally without mentioning theft
Open a covert operation to observe the clerk discreetly
Decline to open an examination on these facts, explain that predication is absent, and propose targeted analytics on the payables data to establish whether any basis exists
p1_s1.e: Lifestyle change and demeanour, without any transactional irregularity, do not amount to predication — a reasonable trained professional would not yet believe fraud occurred. Management authority cannot substitute for it. The constructive path is targeted analytics to establish whether a basis exists. A covert operation and an accusatory interview both require greater predication, and even an 'informal' interview on this footing risks the clerk's rights and the organisation's exposure.

p1_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, analytics later reveal 23 payments to a vendor whose bank account matches the clerk's own. What changes, and what is the correct sequencing from this point?
o: Predication now exists; open the examination, work general to specific, interview least-culpable witnesses first, and reserve any admission-seeking interview until the evidence is corroborated
Refer the matter to police without further internal work
Predication now exists; interview the clerk immediately with an accusation to secure a confession
Nothing changes; the original lack of predication permanently bars an examination
p1_s2.e: The analytics supply predication — an objective, documented basis. The examination then follows the standard sequencing: general → specific, least-culpable → most-culpable, with the admission-seeking interview held back until guilt is reasonably certain and evidence corroborated. An immediate accusation forfeits the informational phase; an absent predication is curable, not a permanent bar; and premature referral without internal groundwork weakens the case.

p1_j4.t: Which action is LEAST appropriate in the initial response to a credible fraud allegation?
o: Engaging counsel so the work proceeds under privilege
Restricting knowledge of the matter to a need-to-know team
Securing and preserving relevant records and system access logs
Circulating an all-staff email asking anyone with information about the suspected employee to come forward
p1_j4.e: A broad all-staff announcement destroys confidentiality, alerts the suspect to destroy evidence, and exposes the organisation to defamation and employment claims. Preserving evidence, restricting knowledge, and working under counsel are all core initial-response steps.

p2_j1.t: A private company's examiner is about to interview an employee suspected of expense fraud. Which statement is CORRECT?
o: The employee has no rights whatsoever in a private investigation
Miranda warnings are not required of a private employer, but the interview must remain genuinely voluntary and free of detention
The employee must be told they will be dismissed if they refuse to answer
Miranda warnings must be given because the interview may lead to prosecution
p2_j1.e: Miranda restrains custodial interrogation by government, so a private employer need not give warnings. That does not confer unlimited power: the interview must be voluntary in fact and appearance, or the employer risks false-imprisonment and coercion claims. Threatening dismissal for silence and asserting the employee has 'no rights' are both legally hazardous and factually wrong.

p2_j2.t: During an interview, an employee stands and says he wants to leave. The examiner positions himself between the employee and the door and says 'we're not finished'. What is the MOST significant legal exposure created?
p2_j2.e: Physically obstructing exit and asserting the employee may not go creates a false imprisonment risk — unlawful restraint of a person's freedom of movement. Defamation concerns publication of untrue statements, breach of contract concerns agreed terms, and malicious prosecution arises from a baseless referral — none matches an obstructed exit.

p2_j3.t: A private examiner is asked by a police detective to search a suspect employee's desk and hand over what she finds, so the police need not obtain a warrant. What is the PRIMARY concern?
o: The desk belongs to the employer, so there is no issue at all
The examiner should first inform the employee
The examiner may be paid for the work
Acting at law enforcement's direction may make the examiner a state actor, importing constitutional search-and-seizure constraints and risking suppression of the evidence
p2_j3.e: A private party acting at the direction of law enforcement can become a state actor, so constitutional protections that would not bind a private employer suddenly apply — and evidence gathered may be suppressed. Employer ownership of the desk answers the private question but not the state-action problem, which is the primary concern here.

p2_d1.t: A municipal employee is told he will be dismissed unless he answers questions that may incriminate him. Separately, a unionised factory worker asks for a representative at an investigatory interview likely to lead to discipline. These invoke, respectively:
p2_d1.e: Garrity protects a public employee from compelled self-incriminating statements under threat of job loss. Weingarten gives a unionised employee the right to request representation at an investigatory interview that may result in discipline. Public-sector compulsion versus union representation is the discriminator.

p2_s1.scenario: A private manufacturer suspects a supervisor of colluding with a supplier. Investigators review his work email and company laptop (both covered by a signed acceptable-use policy stating no expectation of privacy), his company-issued phone, and — without a policy covering it — his personal backpack left in a locked staff locker he supplied himself. During a three-hour interview in a room with the door closed, he twice asks to leave and is told the meeting will continue until he explains the payments. Afterwards, the operations director emails all forty plant staff stating the supervisor is 'under investigation for taking bribes'.
p2_s1.t: Which actions create the MOST significant legal exposure for the employer?
o: The search of the personal backpack in his own locker, the refusal to let him leave the interview, and the all-staff email naming him
The use of a signed acceptable-use policy
Interviewing him at all without police present
The review of work email and the company laptop
p2_s1.e: Three distinct exposures arise: searching a personal effect in an employee-supplied locker with no covering policy (invasion of privacy — a reasonable expectation of privacy survives), refusing to let him leave (false imprisonment), and publishing the allegation to forty colleagues (defamation, absent privilege). The email and laptop review is protected by the acknowledged policy, and no police presence is required for a private interview.

p2_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, which single change would have MOST reduced the employer's overall exposure while preserving the investigation?
o: Obtaining the supervisor's written confession before doing anything else
Having the operations director conduct the interview instead

Keeping the interview voluntary (door unlocked, freedom to leave stated and honoured), limiting the search to property covered by policy, and confining knowledge of the allegation to a need-to-know team
p2_s2.e: The exposures were coercion, an unauthorised personal search, and broad publication — all three are cured by preserving voluntariness, restricting searches to policy-covered property, and confining disclosure to need-to-know. Covert recording adds legal risk in many jurisdictions; swapping interviewers changes nothing; and demanding a confession first inverts the methodology and compounds coercion.

p2_j4.t: Which practice does the MOST to reduce an employee's reasonable expectation of privacy in company computer systems?
o: A clearly published, acknowledged acceptable-use policy stating that systems may be monitored and that no expectation of privacy exists
p2_j4.e: Expectation of privacy is shaped chiefly by notice: a published, acknowledged policy stating systems are monitored and carry no expectation of privacy. Mere ownership of the hardware is weaker than explicit notice, and passwords or encryption are security measures that, if anything, can increase a perceived expectation of privacy.

p3_j1.t: A supplier made a false statement in negotiations, but the buyer had already independently decided to place the order and never read the statement. Which element of common-law fraud is MOST clearly defeated?
p3_j1.e: If the buyer never read or depended on the statement, the victim did not rely on it — and reliance is an essential element. The statement may still have been false, knowingly made, and even material; without reliance the fraud claim fails. This is why 'reliance' is more than a formality.

p3_d1.t: A cashier pockets money from a till she was never authorised to open. A trustee lawfully holding client funds transfers them to his own account. These are, respectively:
p3_d1.e: Taking property the person had no lawful possession of = larceny. Converting property that was lawfully entrusted = embezzlement. The discriminator is how possession began, not who the victim was or how much was taken.

p3_d2.t: Fraudster A tricks a seller into transferring ownership of a car by presenting a forged bank draft. Fraudster B borrows a neighbour's car with permission, then sells it. These are, respectively:
o: False pretences (title obtained by deception) and conversion/embezzlement of entrusted property
p3_d2.e: Obtaining title through a false representation is false pretences. Lawfully receiving possession and then dealing with the property as one's own is conversion/embezzlement. The exam distinguishes title-transferred-by-deception from lawful-possession-then-converted.

p3_j2.t: A billing clerk discovers systematic overbilling of a government health programme and files suit on the government's behalf, standing to share in any recovery. Which statute and mechanism is this?
o: The False Claims Act; a qui tam action by a relator
p3_j2.e: A private relator suing on the government's behalf and sharing the recovery is a qui tam action under the False Claims Act. RICO targets a pattern of racketeering; SOX addresses certification and document destruction; the FCPA addresses foreign bribery and accounting controls.

p3_j3.t: Which fact pattern would MOST likely be charged under RICO rather than a single fraud statute?
o: An ongoing enterprise whose members committed repeated related acts of bribery, extortion and fraud over several years
A one-off forged cheque cashed by an employee
An isolated misstatement in one year's financial statements
p3_j3.e: RICO targets a pattern of racketeering activity conducted through an enterprise — repeated, related predicate acts over time. Single, isolated offences (one cheque, one misstatement, one wire) lack the pattern and enterprise elements that RICO requires.

p3_s1.scenario: A company's purchasing director signed a three-year supply contract after a vendor's sales manager stated the vendor held an exclusive licence for a patented component. That statement was false and the sales manager knew it. Internal emails show the purchasing director had already selected the vendor on price grounds before the statement was made and did not consider the licence claim relevant. The component supplied performed exactly as specified, and the company suffered no measurable loss.
p3_s1.t: Applying the four common-law elements, the fraud claim is MOST likely to fail on which grounds?
o: Reliance and damages — the buyer did not depend on the statement and suffered no loss
Knowledge of falsity, because the manager may have been mistaken
Material false statement, because licences are never material
p3_s1.e: The statement was false and knowingly made, so those elements hold. But the director had already decided on other grounds and did not rely on the claim, and the company suffered no measurable damages — two independent failures, either of which defeats the claim. Licence exclusivity can certainly be material in other circumstances; the problem here is reliance and loss, not materiality in the abstract.

p3_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, suppose instead the director had chosen the vendor because of the exclusivity claim, and the component later failed, costing the company 400,000. Which elements would now be satisfied?
o: None, because the contract was voluntarily signed
All four: a material false statement, knowledge of its falsity, reliance by the victim, and resulting damages
p3_s2.e: On those facts every element is met: the exclusivity claim was material (it drove the selection), knowingly false, relied upon by the director, and produced damages of 400,000. Voluntarily signing a contract does not defeat fraud — that is precisely what a fraudulent inducement produces.

p3_j4.t: Which pairing of trigger phrase to statute is INCORRECT?
o: 'CEO and CFO must certify the financial statements' → False Claims Act
'A relator sues on the government's behalf and shares the recovery' → qui tam / False Claims Act
'Bribing a foreign official to obtain or retain business' → FCPA
p3_j4.e: Executive certification of financial statements is Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX), not the False Claims Act. The other three pairings are correct: RICO for a pattern of racketeering, the FCPA for foreign official bribery, and qui tam under the False Claims Act for relator suits.

p4_j1.t: A defence lawyer argues the prosecution's fraud case must fail because no witness saw the defendant commit the act. Which response is MOST accurate?
o: The argument is correct unless the amount exceeds a statutory threshold
Circumstantial evidence is admissible only if the defendant consents
Most fraud cases are properly built on circumstantial evidence, which is fully admissible and may be more reliable than eyewitness testimony
The argument is correct; fraud requires direct evidence
p4_j1.e: Fraud is concealed by nature, so direct evidence is rare and circumstantial evidence carries most cases — it is fully admissible, and a documented transaction trail is frequently more reliable than a witness's recollection. No consent or monetary threshold governs admissibility.

p4_d1.t: A witness testifies she personally watched the controller alter the ledger. A forensic accountant presents a flowchart she prepared showing how funds moved between accounts. These are, respectively:
o: Direct testimonial evidence and demonstrative evidence
p4_d1.e: An eyewitness account of the act itself is direct testimonial evidence — no inference required. A prepared flowchart explaining other evidence is demonstrative — it illustrates rather than proves the underlying facts.

p4_d2.t: Item A: a witness's account of what a colleague told her the defendant had said, offered to prove the defendant said it. Item B: a purchase ledger created contemporaneously in the ordinary course of business. Regarding admissibility, these are, respectively:
o: Hearsay (generally excluded) and a business record (a recognised hearsay exception)
p4_d2.e: Repeating an out-of-court statement to prove its truth is hearsay, generally excluded. A ledger made contemporaneously in the regular course of business falls within the business records exception and is generally admissible. The discriminator is the reliability that routine business creation supplies.

p4_j2.t: An examiner cannot account for who held a seized laptop for a two-day period. What is the MOST significant consequence?
o: The laptop must be returned to the suspect
Opposing counsel can argue the item could have been altered, potentially rendering the evidence inadmissible
The investigation must be restarted from the beginning
p4_j2.e: A gap in the chain of custody lets the opposing party argue the item could have been altered — they need not prove it was. That risks inadmissibility of what may be the best evidence in the case. Fines, mandatory return, and restarting the investigation are not the standard consequences.

p4_j3.t: Which step does the MOST to preserve attorney-client privilege and work-product protection over an internal fraud investigation?
o: Limiting the investigation to twelve weeks
Conducting the investigation at the direction of legal counsel, with reports addressed to counsel for the purpose of legal advice
Storing files in an encrypted folder
p4_j3.e: Privilege attaches to communications for the purpose of legal advice, and work product to materials prepared in anticipation of litigation — both are best secured by running the engagement at counsel's direction. Labels, encryption, and duration do not create privilege where the legal-advice purpose is absent.

p4_s1.scenario: An examiner investigating procurement fraud assembles: (i) purchase ledgers created in the ordinary course of business; (ii) a colleague's statement about what another employee told her the buyer had said; (iii) emails between the buyer and a vendor; (iv) a summary chart the examiner prepared showing the correlation between the buyer's approvals and the vendor's payments to his wife's account; and (v) a USB drive seized from the buyer's desk, logged into the evidence cabinet on Monday, but with no record of its handling until it was imaged on Thursday.
p4_s1.t: Which item faces the GREATEST admissibility risk, and on what basis?
o: The purchase ledgers, because they are hearsay
The USB drive, because of the three-day gap in the chain of custody
The summary chart, because the examiner prepared it
The emails, because they are circumstantial
p4_s1.e: The unexplained three-day custody gap lets opposing counsel argue the drive could have been altered — the classic chain-of-custody failure and the greatest admissibility risk here. The chart is legitimate demonstrative evidence; the ledgers fall within the business records hearsay exception; and circumstantial emails are fully admissible.

p4_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, the colleague's statement about what another employee reported the buyer said is BEST characterised as:
o: Hearsay, generally excluded if offered to prove the truth of what the buyer said, unless an exception applies
Direct evidence of the buyer's statement
p4_s2.e: This is a second-hand account of an out-of-court statement offered for its truth — hearsay, generally excluded absent an exception. It is not direct evidence of the buyer's words (the colleague did not hear him), and it is neither demonstrative nor real evidence.

p4_j4.t: Which of the following is LEAST likely to be a proper basis for impeaching a witness?
o: Evidence of bias or a financial interest in the outcome
A prior statement inconsistent with the present testimony
The witness's occupation is one the jury may dislike
Impaired capacity to perceive or recall the events
p4_j4.e: Impeachment attacks credibility on legitimate grounds — prior inconsistent statements, bias or interest, and impaired perception or memory. Appealing to prejudice about a witness's occupation is not a proper impeachment basis and invites exclusion as more prejudicial than probative.

p5_j1.t: An examiner takes possession of a suspect's laptop. What should she do FIRST, and why?
o: Boot the laptop and browse recent files to assess relevance
Ask the suspect for the password before doing anything else
Delete temporary files to reduce the data volume
Create a verified forensic image using a write-blocker, recording hash values, and analyse only the copy
p5_j1.e: Booting the original alters last-access times, temporary files and logs, and can render the best evidence inadmissible. The correct first step is a write-blocked forensic image with recorded hash values, analysed as a copy. Deleting anything destroys evidence, and obtaining a password does not precede preservation.

p5_j2.t: Why does an examiner compute hash values before and after imaging digital media?
o: To encrypt the evidence against tampering
To compress the image for storage
To demonstrate the image is bit-for-bit identical to the source and has not been altered, establishing integrity for court
p5_j2.e: A matching hash before and after proves the forensic image is identical to the original and unaltered — the foundation of digital evidence integrity. Hashing does not compress, encrypt, or recover data; those are separate functions.

p5_j3.t: An examiner seizes a suspect's mobile phone at the workplace. Which immediate step is MOST important?
o: Asking the suspect to unlock it
Isolating the device from all networks (airplane mode or a Faraday bag) to prevent remote wiping before imaging
Photographing the home screen for the report
p5_j3.e: A networked phone can be remotely wiped, destroying the evidence entirely. Network isolation is therefore the critical first action. Photographs, charging, and unlocking are secondary and none prevents the catastrophic loss that a remote wipe causes.

p5_d1.t: Standard A: cheques the suspect wrote years before any dispute arose. Standard B: a paragraph the suspect was asked to write out during the investigation. For handwriting comparison these are, respectively:
o: Collected standards (preferred) and requested standards (which may be disguised)
p5_d1.e: Collected standards are naturally written before the dispute and cannot have been disguised — hence preferred. Requested standards are produced on demand and a suspect may deliberately alter their writing. Examiners seek both, but weight collected exemplars more heavily.

p5_d2.t: Technique A recovers impressions left by writing on a sheet that lay above the questioned page. Technique B compares ink formulation and paper watermark against known manufacturing dates. These establish, respectively:
o: Indented writing (recovering unseen content) and document dating (whether it could have existed on its purported date)
p5_d2.e: Indented writing recovers content impressed from a sheet above — revealing what was written, not when. Ink and paper analysis tests whether the document could have existed on its claimed date. One recovers hidden content; the other tests chronology.

p5_s1.scenario: A departing engineer is suspected of taking design files. IT staff, wanting to move quickly, log into his still-active workstation account, browse his documents folder, open several files to check their contents, and copy what looks relevant onto a shared drive. Two days later a forensic examiner is engaged. She finds the original workstation has been used since the suspected exfiltration, no hash values were recorded, and the copied files carry new access timestamps.
p5_s1.t: What is the MOST significant consequence of IT's actions?
o: The files are now duplicated, wasting storage
The original evidence has been altered — access timestamps changed and no verified image or hash exists — seriously undermining integrity and admissibility
The engineer must now be told he is under investigation
Nothing significant; the content of the files is unchanged
p5_s1.e: Browsing and copying from the live machine changed metadata (last-access times), left no write-blocked image, and produced no hash baseline — so the defence can argue the evidence was altered. Content being 'unchanged' misses the point: it is the provable integrity that has been lost, and that is what determines admissibility.

p5_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, what should IT have done on discovering the suspicion?
o: Immediately delete the engineer's access and wipe the machine to prevent further loss
Preserve the workstation untouched, isolate it, and engage a forensic examiner to create a write-blocked, hash-verified image before any examination
Ask the engineer to explain the files before securing them
Copy everything to a shared drive for safekeeping
p5_s2.e: The correct response is to preserve and isolate the device untouched and have a forensic image taken with a write-blocker and recorded hashes before any review. Wiping destroys evidence outright, questioning the suspect first invites destruction elsewhere, and ad-hoc copying is exactly the error that caused the problem.

p5_j4.t: Which practice is LEAST consistent with proper handling of a questioned original document?
o: Placing it in a protective sleeve and logging it into the evidence record
Handling it minimally to preserve fingerprints and indented writing
Highlighting the disputed figures and writing the examiner's initials and date across the face of the document
Obtaining the original rather than a photocopy where possible
p5_j4.e: Writing on, highlighting, or annotating an original destroys its evidentiary integrity and can compromise fingerprint and indented-writing analysis. Protective storage, minimal handling, and preferring originals are all correct practice.

p6_j1.t: An examiner receives a year of payment data and is eager to begin testing. Which step is MOST important before running any analysis?
o: Deciding how results will be presented to management
Verifying the completeness and integrity of the data — control totals, record counts, and date coverage
p6_j1.e: Analysis of incomplete or mis-parsed data produces confident but wrong conclusions, so verifying completeness and integrity comes first — control totals, record counts, and date coverage. Software choice, presentation, and personnel files all follow the data being sound.

p6_j2.t: Which data set is APPROPRIATE for a Benford's Law test?
o: Vendor payment amounts arising from ordinary business activity
Telephone numbers in the vendor master file
p6_j2.e: Benford applies to natural numbers produced by underlying processes, such as payment or invoice amounts. It does not apply to assigned or sequential numbers — employee IDs, cheque numbers, and telephone numbers — which have no reason to follow the distribution.

p6_j3.t: A Benford's analysis of disbursements shows a pronounced spike in amounts beginning '48' and '49'. What is the MOST appropriate conclusion?
o: This is a lead: investigate whether invoices are being split or sized just below a 5,000 approval threshold, and verify before alleging anything
The data set is unsuitable for Benford analysis
Fraud is proven in the disbursement process
The spike is meaningless because Benford concerns only the first digit
p6_j3.e: A Benford deviation flags where to look, never guilt. A cluster just under a round approval limit suggests threshold structuring or invoice splitting, which must then be verified against approval rules and supporting documents. Payment amounts are a valid Benford population, and second-digit and first-two-digit tests are legitimate refinements.

p6_d1.t: Test A searches free-text expense descriptions and emails for language associated with concealment. Test B maps connections between employees, vendors, addresses and bank accounts to reveal hidden relationships. These are, respectively:
p6_d1.e: Textual analytics examines unstructured language for indicative patterns. Visual/link analysis maps relationships between entities to expose concealed connections — the technique that surfaces employee-vendor collusion. Neither is Benford, which concerns digit distribution.

p6_d2.t: Analysis A identifies missing numbers in a sequential range of company cheques. Analysis B identifies payments clustered immediately below a 25,000 approval limit. These are, respectively:
p6_d2.e: Gap testing finds missing items in a sequence — a classic cheque-tampering indicator. Just-below-threshold analysis finds transactions deliberately sized to avoid a higher approval level. Different schemes, different tests.

p6_s1.scenario: An examiner analysing three years of accounts-payable data finds: 61 invoices from one vendor all between 9,100 and 9,850 against a 10,000 approval threshold; four pairs of invoices with identical amounts and dates but different invoice numbers; the vendor's registered bank account matching an employee's payroll account; and a Benford first-digit test showing a marked over-representation of 9s across that vendor's payments. Management asks the examiner to report immediately that the employee committed fraud.
p6_s1.t: What is the MOST appropriate response?
o: Report as requested; four independent analytics agree
Treat the analytics as strong converging leads, verify each finding against source documents and approval records, and report findings of fact without asserting legal guilt
Interview the employee under caution before any verification
Discard the Benford result because payments are not a valid population
p6_s1.e: The analytics converge powerfully, but they remain leads requiring verification against source documents — and a fraud examiner must report facts without opining on legal guilt. Payments are a valid Benford population, so discarding it is wrong, and a cautioned interview before verification inverts the methodology and pre-judges the matter.

p6_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, which single finding provides the STRONGEST direct link between the employee and the vendor?
o: The vendor's registered bank account matching the employee's payroll account
The invoices clustered below the approval threshold
p6_s2.e: The shared bank account ties the vendor's receipts directly to the employee — a concrete relational link. The threshold clustering, duplicates, and Benford deviation all describe suspicious patterns in the payments but do not, by themselves, connect them to a specific person.

p7_j1.t: An examiner needs a suspect's bank account records to trace diverted funds. Which approach is APPROPRIATE?
o: Ask a friend who works at the bank to look them up quietly
Obtain the records through lawful process — consent, subpoena, court order, or other legal authority
Telephone the bank posing as the account holder to obtain the balance and recent transactions
Purchase the records from an online data broker without enquiry
p7_j1.e: Bank records are nonpublic and require lawful process — consent, subpoena, or court order. Pretexting a bank for financial records is unlawful in many jurisdictions; using an insider to bypass controls induces a breach; and buying records without provenance risks trafficking in unlawfully obtained data.

p7_d1.t: Record A: the register of directors and registered office of a supplier company. Record B: the suspect's consumer credit report. These are, respectively:
o: Public (freely obtainable) and nonpublic (requiring a permissible purpose)
p7_d1.e: Corporate registry filings are public and obtainable by anyone — often the fastest way to link an employee to a vendor. A consumer credit report is nonpublic and may be obtained only for a permissible purpose under credit-reporting law.

p7_j2.t: An examiner suspects an employee has an undisclosed interest in a vendor. Which public source is MOST likely to establish the connection quickly and lawfully?
o: Corporate registry filings showing the vendor's directors, shareholders and registered office
p7_j2.e: Corporate registry filings are public and directly reveal directors, shareholders and the registered address — frequently matching an employee's household. Credit reports and phone records are nonpublic and require authority; the vendor's payroll is a third party's private record.

p7_j3.t: An examiner captures a key page from a vendor's website showing a claim later denied. What should she do to make the capture reliable evidence?
o: Record the URL, date and time of capture, preserve a full screenshot or archived copy, and document the method used
Email the link to counsel and rely on that
Print the page without any annotation of source or date
Describe the page from memory in the report
p7_j3.e: Web pages change and disappear, so a capture must be documented with URL, date/time, method and a preserved copy to be reliable. Memory descriptions, a bare link (which may later resolve differently), and an undated printout all fail to establish what the page said when it mattered.

p8_j1.t: A subject reports modest income but has accumulated two unmortgaged properties and pays large school fees in cash. Records of his business are incomplete. Which method is MOST appropriate?
o: The net worth method — the increase in wealth plus living expenses, less known legitimate sources, imputes unreported income
p8_j1.e: Incomplete records rule out reliable direct tracing, and the fact pattern is accumulated wealth plus large living expenses — the signature of the net worth method. Benford tests digit distributions, not income. Bank deposits would fit a subject cycling cash through accounts, which is not what is described.

p8_d1.t: Subject A accumulates property and investments. Subject B spends everything on travel, dining and gambling, accumulating nothing. The MOST suitable indirect methods are, respectively:
o: Expenditures method and net worth method
Net worth method and expenditures method
p8_d1.e: The net worth method captures a subject who accumulates assets. The expenditures method suits a subject who spends without accumulating, because there is no wealth increase to measure — only outgoings exceeding known income.

p8_j2.t: A subject challenges a net worth computation by claiming he had a large cash hoard saved before the period began. What does the examiner MOST need to have done to withstand this?
o: Established a firm, evidenced starting net worth at a fixed date and eliminated likely legitimate sources such as gifts, loans and prior cash
Used the bank deposits method as well
Computed the figures to two decimal places
p8_j2.e: The cash hoard defence is the classic attack on a net worth case, and it is defeated by a firm, evidenced opening net worth plus systematic elimination of legitimate sources (gifts, inheritances, loans, prior savings). Precision, extra witnesses, or a second method do not cure a weak starting point.

p8_d2.t: Approach A follows a specific payment from the company account through two intermediaries to the suspect's account. Approach B infers unreported income from an unexplained rise in wealth. These are, respectively:
o: Direct tracing and an indirect (circumstantial) method
p8_d2.e: Following identified transactions through records is direct tracing. Inferring hidden income from unexplained wealth is an indirect/circumstantial method — used precisely when direct evidence is unavailable.

p8_s1.scenario: A procurement officer earns a declared salary equivalent to 45,000 per year. Over four years his net worth rises by 620,000: an unmortgaged apartment, a second vehicle, and a share portfolio. Living expenses are documented at roughly 55,000 per year from card and utility records. He received no inheritance, and searches reveal no loans. Business records at the vendor suspected of paying him were destroyed in an office move. When interviewed, he says he had saved cash 'over many years' before the period began, kept at home.
p8_s1.t: Which computation applies, and how should the examiner address his explanation?
o: Bank deposits method; accept the explanation as unverifiable
Direct tracing; obtain the destroyed vendor records
Expenditures method; ignore the asset accumulation

Net worth method; test the cash-hoard claim by establishing an evidenced opening net worth and examining his earlier earnings, tax filings and living standard to assess whether such savings were possible
p8_s1.e: Accumulated assets plus documented living expenses with destroyed counterparty records is the net worth method fact pattern. The cash-hoard claim is testable, not merely assertable: an evidenced opening net worth and analysis of his earlier income, tax filings and lifestyle show whether such savings could have existed. Destroyed records cannot be obtained, and the expenditures method ignores the very accumulation that is the evidence.

p8_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, the apartment is registered in his sister's name although he pays all outgoings and occupies it. For tracing purposes this is BEST described as:
o: A likely nominee holding — beneficial ownership resting with the subject despite title in another's name — which should be included and evidenced through payment and occupation records
Irrelevant, since he does not hold legal title
A gift that reduces his net worth
p8_s2.e: Title in a relative's name while the subject funds and occupies the property is the classic nominee holding: beneficial ownership rests with him and belongs in the computation, evidenced by payment and occupancy records. Legal title alone does not defeat tracing, and while the arrangement may support other inferences, describing it as proven laundering overstates what the facts establish.

p9_j1.t: An examiner begins an interview with a warehouse clerk who may have knowledge of a theft but is not a suspect. Which opening is MOST appropriate?
o: Establish rapport, give a neutral reason for the interview, and seek a commitment to cooperate before any fact-gathering
Ask whether he has ever stolen anything in his life
'We know stock is being stolen and we think you're involved — explain yourself'
Present the inventory analysis and ask him to account for every discrepancy
p9_j1.e: The introductory phase establishes rapport, states a neutral purpose, and secures cooperation — it never accuses. Opening with an accusation or a demand to account for discrepancies destroys the informational phase, and a broad character question is both inflammatory and evidentially useless.

p9_d1.t: Question A: 'Walk me through what happened that evening.' Question B: 'You signed the goods-received note that night, didn't you?' These are, respectively:
o: An open question and a leading question
p9_d1.e: Open questions invite a narrative and yield the most information. Leading questions contain their own answer and are used to confirm facts already established — appropriate later, not as a primary fact-gathering tool.

p9_j2.t: Which sequence of interview question types is CORRECT?
p9_j2.e: The correct order is Introductory → Informational → Closing → Assessment → Admission-seeking, with the final two used only when circumstances warrant. Placing assessment or admission-seeking early forfeits the cooperation and information the earlier phases produce.

p9_j3.t: An interviewer wants to reduce an inhibitor to communication in a witness who fears looking foolish for having missed the fraud. Which approach is MOST effective?
o: Interviewing him alongside his manager for context
Reducing ego threat — interviewing privately, normalising the difficulty of detecting such schemes, and framing his help as valuable
Emphasising the seriousness of the consequences for the company
Telling him others have already blamed him
p9_j3.e: Ego threat is the inhibitor here, and it is reduced by privacy, normalising the difficulty, and offering recognition — a facilitator. Stressing consequences heightens anxiety; a manager present amplifies ego threat; and suggesting others blame him is coercive and counterproductive.

p9_j4.t: Which interviewing practice is LEAST appropriate?
o: Interviewing two employees together to save time and let them corroborate each other
Beginning with open questions before narrowing to closed ones
p9_j4.e: Joint interviews let subjects align their accounts, suppress candid disclosure, and destroy independent corroboration — witnesses must be interviewed separately and privately. Contemporaneous documentation and an open-to-closed progression are correct practice.

p10_j1.t: During an admission-seeking interview the subject begins to say 'I didn't take anything—'. What should the interviewer do, and why?
o: Let the denial be fully stated and recorded for the file
Warn him that denial will lead to prosecution
Interrupt and delay the denial before it hardens, because a firmly stated denial is psychologically harder for the subject to retract
p10_j1.e: Skilled interviewers interrupt denials before they entrench — once firmly voiced, a denial becomes a position the subject must defend. Recording the denial hardens it; ending the interview forfeits the opportunity; and threatening prosecution is coercive and may void any resulting statement.

p10_j2.t: Which pair of choices correctly illustrates the alternative question technique?
o: 'Did you take the money, or did someone else?'
'Do you want to confess now, or speak to a lawyer first?'
'Did you plan this from the start, or did it get out of hand after your mother's illness?'
'Are you guilty, or are you innocent?'
p10_j2.e: The alternative question offers two incriminating choices, one more face-saving, so that either answer is an admission. Offering an innocent alternative, a procedural choice, or a bare guilt/innocence question all fail the technique — the subject can simply select the exculpatory option.

p10_j3.t: A subject agrees to sign a written statement. Which practice is INCORRECT?
o: Writing the statement in the subject's own words, including approximate dates and amounts
Having the subject initial any corrections and sign each page
Including the examiner's assurance that the company will not prosecute if the subject signs
Recording that the statement was made voluntarily
p10_j3.e: Never promise leniency or non-prosecution — it exceeds the examiner's authority, misleads the subject, and can render the confession involuntary and inadmissible. The subject's own words, a voluntariness acknowledgment, and initialled corrections are all correct practice.

p10_j4.t: An interviewer notices the subject answering questions with questions and offering character testimony. What is the CORRECT interpretation?
o: They form part of a cluster of possible deception indicators that warrant further probing, but no single cue proves deception
They indicate the subject is confused and the interview should end
p10_j4.e: No single verbal or non-verbal cue proves deception. Cues have value only as clusters that signal where to probe further. Treating them as proof is a serious error, dismissing them entirely wastes information, and ending the interview forfeits the opportunity to test them.

p10_s1.scenario: An examiner has documentary evidence that a store manager processed 47 fictitious refunds totalling 31,000 to a card in his wife's name, corroborated by CCTV and till data. He arranges a private interview in a small office, accompanied by a colleague as witness, and opens by stating directly: 'Our examination shows you processed refunds to your wife's card.' The manager starts to deny it; the examiner talks over the denial and continues. He then says: 'People do this when they are under real pressure. Was this something you planned, or did it start when your wife lost her job?' The manager pauses, then says the second is closer to the truth.
p10_s1.t: Which techniques has the examiner correctly applied?
o: The cognitive interview and criteria-based statement analysis
Reasonable certainty of guilt before accusing, a private setting, a direct accusation, interruption of the denial, a rationalisation theme, and the alternative question
None — the interview was improperly conducted
p10_s1.e: Every step follows the method: reasonable certainty of guilt established by documentary and CCTV evidence, a private setting, a confident direct accusation, interruption of the denial, a rationalisation theme, and an alternative question with two incriminating choices. The manager's response is a benchmark admission. No cognitive interview or statement analysis is described here.

p10_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, the manager now says he will sign whatever is needed 'if this stays internal and the police aren't involved'. What should the examiner do?
o: Agree, since internal resolution is faster and secures the confession
Tell him the police will definitely not be involved to obtain the signature
Decline to give any assurance about prosecution, explain that the decision is not his to make, and take the statement in the subject's own words with a voluntariness acknowledgment
Postpone the statement until management decides on prosecution
p10_s2.e: An examiner must never promise leniency or non-prosecution — the decision is not his, and such a promise can render the confession involuntary and inadmissible, destroying the case. The correct course is to decline the assurance, explain the limits of his authority, and take a voluntary statement in the subject's own words. Postponing risks losing the admission entirely.

p11_j1.t: Before commencing a covert operation, what must the examiner do FIRST?
o: Obtain the informant's promise of confidentiality
Ensure adequate predication exists and commit the basis, objectives and expected information to a written memorandum
Notify the suspect that an investigation is under way
p11_j1.e: Covert operations require adequate predication plus a written memorandum prepared before commencement, recording the basis, objectives and expected information. Notifying the suspect defeats the purpose; confidentiality promises and equipment selection are downstream of the authorising step.

p11_j2.t: An examiner plans surveillance of a suspect. Which approach carries the LOWEST legal risk?
o: Observing the suspect's activity in public areas and recording observations in a contemporaneous log
Using a telephoto lens to photograph inside the suspect's home
Following the suspect into a private members' club by deception
Placing a recording device in the suspect's personal vehicle
p11_j2.e: Observation in public places, where there is no reasonable expectation of privacy, documented in a contemporaneous log, is the lowest-risk approach. Photographing inside a home, placing devices in private property, and gaining entry to private premises by deception all invite privacy, trespass and — depending on jurisdiction — criminal exposure.

p11_d1.t: Person A is a bank employee who routinely provides account-opening information as part of her job, with no expectation of secrecy. Person B secretly supplies information about his employer's fraud on condition his identity is protected. These are, respectively:
p11_d1.e: A source supplies information in the ordinary course of their occupation without confidentiality expectations. An informant provides information confidentially, usually with personal exposure or motive — which is why motive assessment and corroboration matter more with informants.

p11_j3.t: An informant asks the examiner to guarantee that his identity will never be revealed under any circumstances. What is the CORRECT response?
o: Refuse to accept any information from him
Give the guarantee; informant protection is absolute
Give the guarantee verbally but not in writing
Explain that identity will be protected as far as possible, but that a court may compel disclosure, and no absolute guarantee can be given
p11_j3.e: An examiner cannot promise absolute confidentiality, because a court may compel disclosure. The honest position is to protect identity so far as possible while making the limits clear. Giving an unqualified guarantee — in any form — misleads the informant and may expose them to serious harm.

p12_j1.t: Which sentence is MOST appropriate for a fraud examination report?
o: 'The subject is an obviously dishonest individual who showed no remorse.'
'Bank records (Exhibit 7) show 47 transfers totalling 218,000 from the company account to an account in the subject's name.'
'The subject is guilty of embezzlement and should be prosecuted.'
'It is likely the subject stole the money, though we cannot be certain.'
p12_j1.e: A report states facts tied to identified exhibits. Declaring guilt is a legal conclusion reserved to the trier of fact; characterising the subject as dishonest is editorialising; and speculating about likelihood overstates findings without evidential support.

p12_j2.t: An examiner finds evidence that partially exculpates the subject — a signed authorisation for three of the disputed payments. What should the report do?
o: Mention it verbally to management but keep it out of the written report
Include it only if opposing counsel requests it
Omit it, since it weakens the case
Include it fully; omitting exculpatory evidence destroys the examiner's credibility and hands opposing counsel a decisive cross-examination
p12_j2.e: Exculpatory evidence must be included. Omitting it is among the gravest reporting errors: when it surfaces later, the examiner's impartiality and every other finding are impeached. Withholding it pending a request, or confining it to a verbal briefing, is the same failure in another form.

p12_j3.t: Which is the LEAST appropriate content for a fraud examination report?
o: A schedule of transactions cross-referenced to exhibits
A description of the procedures performed
A statement of the scope and any limitations on it
The examiner's personal view that the subject 'has always seemed untrustworthy'
p12_j3.e: A personal characterisation of the subject is editorialising — irrelevant, prejudicial, and damaging to the examiner's impartiality under cross-examination. Scope, cross-referenced schedules, and procedures performed are core report content.

p12_d1.t: Item A: a flow-of-funds diagram the examiner prepared summarising 60 transfers. Item B: the underlying bank statements themselves. In evidentiary terms these are, respectively:
o: Demonstrative evidence (which must accurately represent the underlying proof) and documentary/real evidence
p12_d1.e: A prepared diagram is demonstrative — it explains other evidence and must faithfully represent it. The bank statements are documentary evidence of the transactions themselves. A diagram that overstates or simplifies beyond the statements becomes a liability under cross-examination.

p13_j1.t: A defendant is acquitted of criminal fraud. The victim company then sues civilly on the same facts. Which statement is CORRECT?
o: The civil court must follow the criminal verdict
Only an appeal of the acquittal is possible
The civil suit may proceed, because the civil standard (preponderance) is lower than the criminal standard (beyond a reasonable doubt)
The civil suit is barred by the acquittal
p13_j1.e: Acquittal means the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt; a civil claimant need only show the case is more likely than not. Because the standards differ, the civil action is not barred and the civil court is not bound by the acquittal.

p13_j2.t: Rank the burdens of proof from LOWEST to HIGHEST.
o: Preponderance of the evidence → clear and convincing → beyond a reasonable doubt
Clear and convincing → preponderance → beyond a reasonable doubt
Beyond a reasonable doubt → clear and convincing → preponderance
Preponderance → beyond a reasonable doubt → clear and convincing
p13_j2.e: The ladder runs preponderance of the evidence ('more likely than not') → clear and convincing → beyond a reasonable doubt. Preponderance governs most civil fraud actions; beyond a reasonable doubt governs criminal prosecutions.

p13_d1.t: Process A: a neutral third party hears both sides and issues a binding determination. Process B: a neutral facilitates negotiation but cannot impose an outcome. These are, respectively:
p13_d1.e: Arbitration produces a binding determination by the arbitrator. Mediation is facilitative — the mediator helps the parties reach their own settlement and cannot impose one. The discriminator is whether the neutral decides.

p13_d2.t: System A relies on judge-made precedent with an adversarial trial. System B applies codified statutes with a more active, inquisitorial judge. These are, respectively:
p13_d2.e: Common law is precedent-based and adversarial; civil law is code-based and inquisitorial, with the judge taking a more active investigative role. Note that 'civil law' as a system is distinct from 'civil actions' as a type of proceeding — a deliberate exam ambiguity.

p13_j3.t: An organisation faces both a criminal investigation and a civil suit arising from the same fraud. What is the PRIMARY risk of these parallel proceedings?
o: The criminal case is automatically stayed
Civil discovery may compel disclosures that create self-incrimination exposure in the criminal matter, requiring careful coordination
The organisation must choose which to defend
Damages cannot be awarded until the criminal case concludes
p13_j3.e: The principal hazard in parallel proceedings is that civil discovery compels disclosure that may be used in the criminal case — creating self-incrimination exposure that must be managed (sometimes by seeking a stay). The organisation cannot simply decline to defend one, and neither proceeding is automatically suspended.

p13_s1.scenario: A company discovers a former finance manager diverted 900,000. Prosecutors open a criminal file. The company also wants its money back and is considering options: a civil claim for damages and restitution, a claim on its fidelity bond, and internal disciplinary findings that are now moot since he has resigned. Counsel notes the criminal case may take two years, during which the manager could dissipate assets. The manager has offered to attend arbitration.
p13_s1.t: Which combination BEST protects the company's recovery position?
o: Pursue the civil claim in parallel — seeking interim freezing/restraint relief to prevent dissipation — while notifying the fidelity bond insurer within policy deadlines
Rely solely on the criminal court to order restitution
Accept arbitration as the sole route because it is faster
Wait for the criminal verdict, then sue
p13_s1.e: Recovery is protected by acting in parallel: a civil claim with interim freezing relief stops dissipation during the years the criminal case runs, and fidelity bond notice must be given within policy deadlines or cover is lost. Waiting risks the assets vanishing; criminal restitution is uncertain and subordinate to sentencing; and arbitration alone forgoes both interim relief and the bond.

p13_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, the manager is later acquitted at criminal trial. What is the effect on the civil claim?
o: The civil claim may still succeed, because it requires proof only on the balance of probabilities rather than beyond a reasonable doubt
The civil court is bound by the acquittal's findings
The company must repay any interim relief obtained
The civil claim must be dismissed
p13_s2.e: Acquittal establishes only that guilt was not proved beyond a reasonable doubt. The civil claim proceeds on the preponderance standard and may well succeed on the same evidence — the classic consequence of the differing burdens. The civil court is not bound by the criminal findings.

p14_j1.t: Under cross-examination the examiner is asked: 'So in your opinion, the defendant is guilty of fraud?' What is the CORRECT response?
o: Restate the findings within expertise — what the records show — and explain that whether that constitutes the offence is for the court to determine
'That is a matter for my client to answer.'
'I cannot answer any questions about my findings.'
p14_j1.e: An examiner must never opine on legal guilt or innocence. The correct answer restates the factual findings within expertise and leaves the legal conclusion to the trier of fact. Refusing to discuss findings at all is evasive and damages credibility; deflecting to the client is not a proper answer.

p14_d1.t: Witness A testifies she saw the manager remove cash from the safe. Witness B, a qualified forensic accountant, testifies that in her opinion the accounting records were manipulated to conceal a shortfall. These are, respectively:
o: A lay witness (facts personally observed) and an expert witness (opinion within expertise)
An expert witness and a lay witness
p14_d1.e: A lay witness testifies to what she personally perceived. An expert, once qualified, may offer opinions within her field — such as whether records show manipulation. The discriminator is whether the testimony is observation or qualified opinion.

p14_j2.t: On cross-examination, opposing counsel establishes that the examiner did not review three months of records that were unavailable. What is the BEST response?
o: Argue with counsel about the relevance of those records
Claim the records would not have changed anything, without explanation
Concede the limitation directly, state that it was disclosed in the report's scope section, and explain what effect (if any) it has on the conclusions
p14_j2.e: Conceding a genuinely true point preserves credibility, especially where the limitation was already disclosed in the report's scope. Denying an obvious limitation, arguing with counsel, or making an unsupported assertion that nothing would change all damage the examiner far more than the limitation itself.

p14_j3.t: Which practice would MOST undermine an examiner's effectiveness as an expert witness?
o: Acknowledging the limits of one's expertise
Explaining findings in plain language a jury can follow
Advocating for the retaining party's position and resisting every concession
Ensuring every opinion has a reasonable evidential basis
p14_j3.e: An expert is a witness, not an advocate. Arguing the retaining party's case and refusing all concessions signals bias and destroys credibility with the trier of fact. Plain language, candour about limits, and an evidential basis for every opinion are the marks of an effective expert.

p14_s1.scenario: A CFE is called as an expert in a civil fraud trial. On cross-examination, counsel asks a series of rapid questions demanding yes-or-no answers, including: 'You were paid by the plaintiff, weren't you?'; 'You never interviewed my client, did you?'; 'You did not review the 2023 subsidiary ledgers, correct?'; and finally 'So you cannot rule out an innocent explanation, can you?' The examiner's report had disclosed that the subsidiary ledgers were withheld by the defendant and that the defendant declined to be interviewed.
p14_s1.t: Which approach BEST preserves the examiner's credibility?
o: Concede each factually true point, and where a yes/no answer would mislead, politely insist on completing the answer — noting that the ledgers were withheld and the interview was declined
Answer only 'yes' or 'no' to every question as instructed, volunteering nothing
Refuse to answer questions about payment as irrelevant
Argue that counsel is being unfair to the examination
p14_s1.e: Each proposition is factually true and should be conceded — fighting them signals bias. But a bare 'no' to 'you did not review the ledgers' would mislead, since the defendant withheld them; the examiner may politely insist on completing the answer. Refusing to address the fee question suggests something to hide, and arguing with counsel forfeits the neutrality that makes an expert persuasive.

p14_s2.t: Referring to the same scenario, counsel's final question — 'So you cannot rule out an innocent explanation, can you?' — is best answered by:
o: Declining to answer on the grounds that it calls for a legal conclusion
'Yes, I can rule it out completely.'
Acknowledging that ruling out every conceivable explanation is not the examiner's role, and stating what the evidence examined does and does not show, leaving the conclusion to the court
p14_s2.e: The question invites either an overstatement or a damaging bare concession. The correct course is to explain that exhaustively excluding all explanations is not the examiner's function, state what the examined evidence shows and does not show, and leave the ultimate conclusion to the court. Claiming to rule everything out is indefensible; a bare 'no' distorts; and the question is answerable within expertise, so declining entirely is evasive.

q1_x1.t: Which best distinguishes forensic accounting from a fraud examination?
o: Fraud examination is broader and includes valuation and damages work
Forensic accounting may only be performed by auditors
Forensic accounting is the broader application of accounting skills to matters that may lead to litigation; fraud examination is the narrower discipline of resolving a specific fraud allegation
q1_x1.e: Forensic accounting spans any accounting work anticipating litigation — valuation, damages, bankruptcy, matrimonial. Fraud examination is the narrower methodology for resolving a fraud allegation. Every fraud examination may involve forensic accounting; not every forensic engagement is a fraud examination.

q1_x2.t: When should an organisation prepare its fraud response plan?
o: After the first external audit finding
Immediately after a fraud is discovered, tailored to that matter
In advance of any incident, defining roles, escalation and evidence-preservation steps
q1_x2.e: A fraud response plan is prepared in advance, so that when an allegation arises the organisation already knows who leads, who is notified, how evidence is preserved, and how confidentiality is maintained. Drafting one during a live incident guarantees delay, contamination of evidence, and inconsistent decisions.

q1_x3.t: Examiner A reviews the entire procurement process before looking at any individual. Examiner B begins by interviewing the named suspect. Regarding examination methodology these approaches are, respectively:
o: General-to-specific (correct methodology) and an approach that inverts the standard sequence
q1_x3.e: Examinations proceed general → specific: understand the process, then narrow to the person. Beginning with the suspect forfeits the informational phase, risks alerting them, and leaves the examiner without corroboration when it matters most.

q2_x1.t: An employer wishes to search employee lockers for stolen stock. Which factor MOST determines whether this is lawful?
o: Whether a published policy reduced the expectation of privacy in those lockers and whether the lockers are employer-supplied
Whether the employee is a suspect
q2_x1.e: Lawfulness turns on the reasonable expectation of privacy, which is shaped by whether the employer supplied the locker and whether a published policy put employees on notice that lockers may be searched. Value of the goods, suspect status, and police presence do not create search authority — indeed police involvement may import constitutional constraints.

q2_x2.t: An organisation dismisses an employee for fraud and tells a prospective employer he 'is a thief', without having proved the allegation. What is the PRIMARY exposure?
o: Defamation — publication of an unproven allegation to a third party without privilege
q2_x2.e: Communicating an unproven allegation to a third party outside any privilege creates defamation exposure. False imprisonment concerns restraint of movement, malicious prosecution concerns baseless legal proceedings, and breach of confidence concerns misuse of confidential information.

q2_x3.t: Employer A searches a company laptop covered by an acknowledged acceptable-use policy. Employer B searches an employee's personal mobile phone with no policy coverage and no consent. Regarding privacy exposure these are, respectively:
o: Low risk (expectation of privacy reduced by notice) and high risk (personal device, no notice or consent)
q2_x3.e: An acknowledged policy reduces the expectation of privacy in company systems, making that search defensible. A personal device with no policy or consent retains a strong expectation of privacy — searching it invites a privacy claim regardless of suspicion.

q3_x1.t: Which element of common-law fraud is MOST often decisive where a defendant claims they genuinely believed their statement was true?
q3_x1.e: A genuine belief in the statement's truth attacks knowledge of falsity — the scienter element. The statement may still be false, relied upon, and damaging, but without knowledge of its falsity when made, the fraud claim fails (though negligent misrepresentation may remain available).

q3_x2.t: Two employees agree to submit false invoices, and one of them creates the first fake invoice. Separately, an employee alone forges a single cheque. In legal terms the first involves an additional charge of:
o: Conspiracy — an agreement between two or more, typically with an overt act in furtherance
q3_x2.e: An agreement between two or more persons to commit an unlawful act, coupled with an overt act in furtherance, constitutes conspiracy — a charge available in addition to the substantive offence. The lone forger has no agreement and therefore no conspiracy.

q3_x3.t: Which statute is characterised by the phrase 'scheme to defraud together with use of the mail or interstate wires'?
q3_x3.e: Mail and wire fraud require a scheme to defraud plus use of the mails or wires in furtherance — extremely broad federal hooks used across fraud prosecutions. RICO requires a pattern through an enterprise; SOX addresses certification and document destruction; the FCA addresses false claims to government.
